Core Concept: Sometimes our thoughts and feelings get really noisy — like a radio with too much static. Today we practise noticing when we feel like ourselves versus when we feel a bit lost or scrambled.
Opening Hook: Can anyone tell me about a time they felt really, really good — like everything just felt right? What were you doing?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine your brain is a radio. When you tune it just right, you hear the music clearly. When it's on the wrong station, it's just crackle and noise. Today we practise finding your station.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: Have you ever seen a lighthouse? Even in a really big storm with waves crashing and wind howling, the lighthouse light just keeps going — steady and calm. You have something like that light inside you too.
Teaching Points: 1. Everyone has big feelings and busy thoughts — that's normal and okay. | 2. Some feelings are like signals — they tell us something true about what we need or want. | 3. Some feelings are like static — messy and confusing, usually when we're tired or scared or trying too hard to fit in. | 4. Today we just start noticing the difference — and that's a superpower.
Experiential Exercise: THE FEELINGS DIAL: Draw a big circle like a radio dial. On one side write 'SIGNAL' and draw a smiley face. On the other write 'NOISE' and draw a wiggly face. Think of a feeling you had this week. Was it signal or noise? Draw or write it on the right side of the dial. Share with the group if you want to.
Guided Reflection: Let's all sit quietly for one minute. Close your eyes if you want to. Think of a moment this week where you felt happy, safe, or really yourself. Put your hand on your heart. That feeling? That's your signal. Remember what it feels like.
Journaling Prompt: Draw a picture of what it looks like inside your head when you feel calm and good.
Weekly Practice (Mon): Notice when you feel 'signal' today — tell someone about it!
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about one time this week you felt really like yourself.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Come back ready to share one 'signal moment' from your week.
Core Affirmation: My feelings are talking to me, and I'm learning to listen.
Video Description: YouTube: Daniel Siegel 'The Whole Brain Child' animated explanation — how emotions work in the brain, made accessible for children. Runtime ~5 min. Companion book: 'What To Do When You Worry Too Much' by Dawn Huebner.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A child's bedroom — toys everywhere, thoughts swirling like cartoon clouds above their head. VOICE (warm, gentle): 'Sometimes it feels really noisy in here, doesn't it?' CUT TO: The child takes a slow breath. The clouds slow down. One cloud glows — it's a happy memory. VOICE: 'That glowing one? That's your signal. You've always had it.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE — Tune Into Your Inner Self.
Facilitator Notes: Use visuals and movement where possible. Keep reflection time SHORT — 30 seconds max for young children. Story time recommended: ask children to bring a book about feelings for next week.

Core Concept: We all have little voices in our head that say things about us — sometimes kind things, sometimes not-so-kind things. Today we meet those voices and find out where they came from.
Opening Hook: Has anyone ever had a thought like 'I'm not good at that' or 'that's not for me' — and wondered where it came from?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine you have a tiny invisible backpack you carry everywhere. Inside it are all the things people have ever said to you, or things that happened that made you feel a certain way about yourself. Today we look inside the backpack.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: There's a story about a baby elephant tied to a small post. As a baby it tried to pull free, couldn't, and eventually stopped trying. Years later, fully grown, the elephant stays next to the tiny post without even pulling. The rope hasn't changed. The elephant has. We carry stories the same way.
Teaching Points: 1. Everyone has an inner voice — the thoughts we have about ourselves. | 2. Some of those thoughts come from things that happened to us — things people said, or times we felt embarrassed or not good enough. | 3. Those thoughts aren't always true. They're just old stories we started carrying. | 4. Just because a thought is old and loud doesn't mean it's right.
Experiential Exercise: BACKPACK ACTIVITY: Each child gets a paper 'backpack' outline to draw on. Inside the backpack, draw or write 2 things you believe about yourself — one good thing, one thing that sometimes makes you feel bad. Around the outside of the backpack, write where you learned it (e.g. 'school,' 'a friend said,' 'something that happened'). Share the good thing with the group. The harder thing is private unless they choose to share.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes and imagine your backpack. Now imagine taking out the heavy thing — the not-so-kind thought — and looking at it. Who put it there? When? Now imagine a kind, wise grown-up taking it from you and saying: 'You don't have to carry this. It was never yours to carry.'
Journaling Prompt: Draw a picture of yourself WITHOUT the heavy thing in your backpack. What do you look like?
Weekly Practice (Mon): Notice one kind thought about yourself today. Write it down or tell someone.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up one thing in your 'backpack' — something you believe about yourself, good or tricky.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring your backpack drawing back and be ready to share one thing from it.
Core Affirmation: I get to choose which stories I carry.
Video Description: YouTube: 'The Most Magnificent Thing' read-aloud — story about a girl who tries and fails and learns to persist. Runtime ~8 min. Companion book: 'What Do You Do With a Problem?' by Kobi Yamada.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A cartoon child carrying a big backpack, walking slowly. VOICE (gentle): 'Inside that backpack are stories. Some of them are beautiful. Some of them are really heavy.' CUT TO: Child sets the backpack down and looks inside. VOICE: 'Not everything that's heavy belongs to you.' CUT TO: Child stands up taller, backpack lighter, walking forward. FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: Use physical props if possible — a real small backpack to put cards in works wonderfully. Ensure children know they don't have to share private thoughts. Have a quiet corner available.

Core Concept: Sometimes we do things we didn't really mean to — like snap at someone or say something unkind — almost before we even knew we were doing it. Today we learn a superpower: the pause.
Opening Hook: Has anyone ever said or done something, and then straight away wished they hadn't? Tell me about what that feels like in your body — tummy? chest? face?
Signal Metaphor: You know the remote control for the TV? It has a pause button. YOUR brain has one too — it just takes practice to find it. Today we find it.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, the wisest characters — the ones who could solve the hardest problems — were always the ones who could be still. Not frozen. Still. There's a difference. Stillness is a superpower.
Teaching Points: 1. When something upsets us, our brain sends a really fast 'danger' signal — almost like a fire alarm going off. | 2. When that happens, we might yell, hide, cry, or freeze — before we even think about it. | 3. That's not bad or wrong — it's just our brain doing its job. | 4. But here's the cool thing: we can learn to press PAUSE — take one breath, count to three, notice the feeling — and then decide what to do next. That pause is a superpower. Really.
Experiential Exercise: THE PAUSE BUTTON ACTIVITY: Everyone gets a card with a big PAUSE symbol on it. Practise the pause together: Clap hands once (the trigger). Everyone presses their 'pause button' card against their heart and counts 1-2-3 slowly while breathing. Role play: Facilitator pretends to say something frustrating. Children press pause, count, breathe, then decide how to respond. Practise 3 times. Make it fun and slightly silly.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes and imagine you have a real pause button — glowing, right in the middle of your chest. Think of something that happened this week that made you feel big, fast feelings. Now imagine pressing the pause button. What happens in your body when you do?
Journaling Prompt: Draw your pause button. What colour is it? What does it look like? Where on your body would it be?
Weekly Practice (Mon): When you feel a big, fast feeling today, try pressing your imaginary pause button before you react.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Teach someone at home about the pause button. Show them how it works.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring your pause button drawing and a story about one time you tried to use it!
Core Affirmation: When I feel a big feeling, I can pause. I am in charge of what happens next.
Video Description: YouTube: 'Sesame Street — Common and Colbie Caillat: Belly Breathe' — fun, accessible breathing and pause technique for young children. Runtime ~3 min. Companion book: 'When Sophie Gets Angry — Really, Really Angry' by Molly Bang.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A cartoon child is about to stomp off after something annoying happens. VOICE: 'Can you see the moment? Right there — just before the storm?' CUT TO: The child's hand moves to their chest. Press. Pause. 1-2-3. VOICE: 'That's the pause button. Everyone has one.' CUT TO: The child makes a different choice. Smiles a little. VOICE: 'And the more you use it, the stronger it gets.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The pause button card is a tangible anchor children can take home. Coordinate with parents to reinforce the language at home. Make the role-play fun so children associate it with positive feelings.

Weekly Theme: What Your Body Is Telling You
Core Concept: Our bodies are amazing messengers! They tell us when we're scared, excited, tired, or happy — all with feelings inside our body. Today we learn to listen to those feelings.
Opening Hook: Can you show me what your body looks like when you're really happy? Now scared. Now proud. Did you notice your BODY changes when your feelings change? Feelings live in the body!
Signal Metaphor: Your body is like a feelings weather station — it has instruments to help you know what's happening inside. A tummy that flips might mean butterflies of excitement or worry. A tight chest might mean you need a hug. Today we learn to read the weather report.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: There's an old idea that our body, heart, and mind are all connected — like a three-part team. When they're all working together, we feel strong and good. When one part is ignored, we get wobbly. Today we check in with the whole team.
Teaching Points: 1. Feelings start in the body — before you even have a word for them. | 2. A tummy that feels wobbly might mean excited OR nervous — and you can learn to tell the difference! | 3. Listening to your body helps you know what you need: rest, fun, a hug, a drink of water, or just to say what's on your mind. | 4. Your body is your friend and it's always trying to help you.
Experiential Exercise: FEELINGS WEATHER STATION: Each child gets a body outline. Facilitator calls out feelings: happy, scared, excited, tired, proud, embarrassed, angry, loved. Children colour or mark where they feel each one in their body. Share: 'Where do YOU feel happy? Where do you feel nervous?' Discuss: we all feel things in slightly different places — and that's amazing!
Guided Reflection: Let's do a feelings check-in together. Breathe slowly three times. Then: 'What is your body telling you right now?' Put your hands on your belly. What does it feel like? Wobbly? Still? Warm? Tight? That's information. Your body is talking. We're learning to listen.
Journaling Prompt: Draw what your body looks like on the inside when you feel your favourite feeling.
Weekly Practice (Mon): Three times today, ask yourself: 'What is my body telling me right now?' Tell a friend what you find!
Weekly Practice (Wed): Ask a grown-up: 'Where do YOU feel nervous in your body?' Compare answers!
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back your feelings body map and share one new thing you discovered about your feelings.
Core Affirmation: My body helps me understand my feelings. We are a great team.
Video Description: YouTube: 'Emotions and the Brain for Kids' — fun animated explanation of how emotions work in the body. Runtime ~5 min. Companion book: 'The Colour Monster' by Anna Llenas — beautiful exploration of identifying feelings through colour.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: Animated body outline. Different feelings light up different parts — glowing yellow for happy, blue for sad, red for angry. VOICE (warm, playful): 'Did you know feelings don't just live in your head? They live ALL over!' CUT TO: Child touching tummy — the butterflies glow there. VOICE: 'Your body is the most amazing feelings machine. And it's always trying to help you.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: Body map activity is highly engaging — use lots of colour. Keep the focus entirely on internal feelings, never on appearance. The 'feelings weather station' language can be used throughout the whole year as a check-in tool.

Weekly Theme: The Mirror — How We See Ourselves
Core Concept: Have you ever looked in a funny mirror that made you look tall or wiggly or squished? Today we think about the mirror we use to look at ourselves — and make sure it's a good, true one.
Opening Hook: If I drew a picture of you, what would I need to include to make it REALLY you? Not just what you look like — what makes you YOU?
Signal Metaphor: Some mirrors in your head show you looking great. Some show you looking terrible. And sometimes neither is completely true! Today we find the mirror that shows the REAL you — with all the good stuff AND the stuff that's still growing.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: There's an old story about a lion cub raised by sheep. It grew up thinking it was a sheep — timid and small. Until one day it saw its reflection in a river and heard a real lion roar. The cub had always been a lion. It just didn't have the right mirror. You might be missing some things about yourself too.
Teaching Points: 1. Everyone is amazing at some things and still learning at others — and BOTH are true at the same time. | 2. Sometimes when we look at ourselves we only see the hard stuff — the mistakes, the things we can't do yet. | 3. Sometimes we only want to see the good stuff and we don't want to hear when something needs to get better. | 4. The best mirror is honest AND kind — it shows our real strengths AND the places we're still growing.
Experiential Exercise: THE TRUE MIRROR ACTIVITY: Each child draws a large mirror outline. On the LEFT side: draw or write 3 things you're genuinely good at or proud of. On the RIGHT side: draw or write 1 thing you're still learning or working on — this is brave! Decorate the frame with things that matter to you. Share your mirror with the group — at least one thing from each side.
Guided Reflection: Look at your mirror drawing. Now close your eyes and imagine a really wise, kind grown-up looking at you and saying: 'I see all of this, and I think you are wonderful AND still growing. Both of those are true. Both of those are good.' How does that feel?
Journaling Prompt: Draw or write about something you're proud of about yourself that you don't talk about very much.
Weekly Practice (Mon): Tell yourself one true kind thing today. Then tell someone else one true kind thing about THEM.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Ask a grown-up: 'What do you think I'm really good at?' Write it on the frame of your mirror.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring your mirror drawing back and add something new you discovered about yourself this week!
Core Affirmation: I can see myself clearly — the strong parts AND the growing parts. Both of them are me.
Video Description: YouTube: 'The Dot' read-aloud by Peter H. Reynolds — a child discovers their own creativity and ability through brave action. Runtime ~8 min. Companion book: 'I Am Enough' by Grace Byers — affirming picture book about being exactly who you are.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A child holds up a drawing of themselves — small, uncertain. VOICE: 'This is how they see themselves today.' CUT TO: The drawing slowly fills in more details — colours, strengths, a smile. VOICE: 'But there's so much more that's already there.' CUT TO: Child looking at the finished drawing, surprised and pleased. VOICE: 'The mirror only shows the real you when you're brave enough to look properly.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The mirror craft is a session highlight — prepare materials in advance. Emphasise that BOTH strengths AND growing areas belong in the mirror — this normalises ongoing growth. Display mirrors on the room walls with permission — creates a powerful visual of collective self-awareness.

Core Concept: Sometimes we look at other people and wish we were more like them — that we had what they had or could do what they can do. Today we learn why comparing isn't as useful as it feels, and what to do instead.
Opening Hook: Has anyone ever wished they could do something that someone else can do? What does it feel like in your tummy when you compare yourself to someone else?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine everyone has a different-shaped puzzle. Your puzzle is yours — and only your pieces fit it. When you try to compare your puzzle to someone else's, the pieces don't fit and it gets confusing. Today we focus on finding YOUR puzzle pieces.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: There's an old idea about flowers: a daisy doesn't look at a rose and wish it were a rose. A daisy is a perfect daisy. When it tries to be a rose, it forgets to be what it is. You are already your own kind of flower. And that's brilliant.
Teaching Points: 1. Everyone is good at different things — and that's what makes people interesting! | 2. When we compare ourselves to others, we usually only look at the thing they're good at and forget all the amazing things we can do. | 3. Comparing can make us feel bad without actually helping us get better at anything. | 4. What DOES help is looking at how much WE have grown — comparing ourselves to who we were yesterday, not who someone else is today.
Experiential Exercise: YOUR AMAZING PUZZLE: Each child gets a puzzle outline with 4–6 large pieces. In each piece, draw or write one thing you're good at, one thing you love, one thing that makes you you. Look at your completed puzzle: no two are the same! That's the point. Share: 'One piece of my puzzle that's completely unique to me is...'
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think of one thing you can do now that you couldn't do a year ago. It doesn't have to be big. Maybe you can read harder books, ride a bike, make a new friend, or be kinder when you're having a bad day. That's YOUR growth. Nobody else's. It belongs completely to you.
Journaling Prompt: Draw or write about something you've gotten better at this year. How did it make you feel to notice that?
Weekly Practice (Mon): Each time you catch yourself wishing you were more like someone else, ask: 'I wonder what I'm good at that they might not be?'
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up one thing you've gotten better at this year that you're really proud of.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring your puzzle back and add one new piece — something new you noticed about what makes you, you!
Core Affirmation: I am my own kind of amazing. My puzzle is exactly right for me.
Video Description: YouTube: 'You Are Special' by Max Lucado read-aloud — a beautiful story about where worth really comes from. Runtime ~8–10 min.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A field of different flowers — each one different, all beautiful. VOICE: 'What if a daisy tried to be a rose? It would forget to be a daisy.' CUT TO: A daisy, fully open, glowing in morning light. VOICE: 'You are already the most complete version of you. Growing into MORE of yourself — not into someone else.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The puzzle activity is very popular with this age group — make the puzzle pieces large enough for drawing. Celebrate the uniqueness of every puzzle loudly and genuinely. Avoid any competitive element in sharing.

Core Concept: Sometimes we have a mean little voice in our head that says unkind things about us — like 'you can't do that' or 'you're not good enough.' Today we find out that this voice isn't telling the truth — and we learn to find the kinder, truer voice.
Opening Hook: Has anyone ever had a thought like 'I can't do this' right before trying something hard? Where do you think that thought comes from?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine there's a grumpy little gremlin who lives in your head and loves to say negative things. He's loud and sometimes scary — but actually he's tiny and not very bright. Today we meet the gremlin, figure out why he's there, and decide he doesn't get to be the boss.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories the wisest characters always had to face a trickster — a creature who tried to confuse them and make them doubt themselves. The trick was always the same: the trickster has no real power once you name him. 'I see you.' That's all it takes.
Teaching Points: 1. Everyone has a 'worry voice' or 'mean voice' sometimes — it's normal and doesn't make you a bad person. | 2. That voice usually shows up when we're trying something new or scary — because it's trying in a clumsy way to protect us from being hurt. | 3. But the voice isn't very smart — it can't tell the difference between 'genuinely dangerous' and 'just new.' | 4. We can notice the voice, say hello, and then listen to our KINDER inner voice instead — the one that sounds like a true friend.
Experiential Exercise: MEET THE GREMLIN: Everyone draws their 'inner critic gremlin' — what does yours look like? Name it (e.g. Doubty, Grumpy Gus, The Worrier). Now write or draw one thing your gremlin says a lot. Now draw or write what your 'inner friend voice' says instead — the kindest, most honest thing. Share your gremlin's name with the group — the sillier the better!
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Imagine your gremlin — small, grumpy, standing on your shoulder. Hear what it says. Then look at it and say inside your head: 'I see you, [gremlin name]. You don't have to run things today.' Now imagine your kind inner friend voice — warm, sure, on your side. What does it say?
Journaling Prompt: Draw a comic strip: Panel 1 — the gremlin speaks. Panel 2 — you notice it. Panel 3 — you choose the kind voice instead.
Weekly Practice (Mon): Every time you hear your gremlin today, give it a name and then listen for the kinder voice.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about your gremlin and give it a name. Ask them if they have one too!
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring your gremlin drawing and your 'kind voice' back to share with the group!
Core Affirmation: I have a grumpy gremlin AND a kind friend inside me. I choose to listen to the friend.
Video Description: YouTube: 'Beautiful Oops' read-aloud — story about characters with inner critics learning to change perspective. Runtime ~8 min. Companion book: 'Wemberly Worried' by Kevin Henkes — a mouse who worries about everything and learns she is more than her worries.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: Cartoon child with a tiny grumpy gremlin on their shoulder, whispering negative things. VOICE: 'Everyone has a gremlin. Some are louder than others.' CUT TO: The child looks at the gremlin. Smiles. 'I see you, Doubty.' Gremlin shrinks a little. Looks surprised. VOICE: 'You can't un-have the gremlin. But you can choose who gets the microphone.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: Children LOVE naming their gremlin — the sillier the name the better, as it immediately reduces the power of the voice. Display gremlin drawings on the wall throughout Phase 1. Remind children the gremlin is not bad or wrong to have — it's just not the boss.

Weekly Theme: Beneath the Surface — Emotions as Data
Core Concept: Feelings are like messages your heart sends you. Sometimes the messages are easy to understand — 'I'm happy!' or 'I'm sad.' But sometimes feelings are tricky and hidden, like treasure buried under sand. Today we learn to dig and find what's really there.
Opening Hook: Has anyone ever been in a bad mood and not quite known WHY? Or been really angry but not sure what you were actually upset about? That's the feelings iceberg! Today we dig under the surface.
Signal Metaphor: Imagine feelings are like an iceberg. The part you can see above the water is the easy bit — 'I'm angry!' But under the water there's a lot MORE going on — maybe you're actually scared, or hurt, or lonely. Today we look under the water.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: There's an old story about a mother bird who always knew what her babies needed — even before they knew themselves. She didn't fix it — she listened to the sounds they made. Different sounds meant different things. You are your own mother bird. Your feelings are always making sounds. Today we learn the language.
Teaching Points: 1. Big feelings like anger or grumpiness sometimes have smaller, sadder feelings hiding underneath them. | 2. It's okay — and brave — to look underneath and find out what's really there. | 3. When you find the real feeling, it usually gets a little easier to carry. | 4. You don't always have to fix the feeling — sometimes just knowing what it is makes it feel better.
Experiential Exercise: THE FEELINGS ICEBERG: Everyone gets an iceberg drawing — a triangle shape with half above the 'water line' and half below. Above the water: draw or write the feeling everyone can see when you're upset (e.g. angry, grumpy, quiet). Below the water: draw or write what might really be there underneath (e.g. scared, lonely, tired, embarrassed). Facilitator shares an example first. Share: 'Above my waterline, people might see...'
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think of the last time you felt a big feeling that was confusing. Now imagine it like an iceberg. The top part — what everyone could see. The bottom part — what was really going on inside. You don't have to tell anyone the bottom part. Just being brave enough to look is enough.
Journaling Prompt: Draw your feelings iceberg for today. What's above the water? What might be underneath?
Weekly Practice (Mon): When you feel a big feeling today, whisper to yourself: 'I wonder what's really going on underneath?'
Weekly Practice (Wed): Show a grown-up your iceberg drawing and explain it to them. Ask them to draw their iceberg too!
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring a new iceberg drawing showing a feeling you had this week. What did you find underneath?
Core Affirmation: When I look underneath my feelings, I find the real message. And I am brave enough to look.
Video Description: YouTube: 'Inside Out emotions explained for kids' — short clips from Pixar's Inside Out explaining how different emotions work together. Runtime ~3–5 min for clips. Companion book: 'The Feelings Book' by Todd Parr — bright, simple, inclusive celebration of the full range of feelings.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: Animated iceberg. The tip visible above gentle waves — labelled 'ANGRY.' VOICE: 'That's what everyone sees...' CUT TO: Underwater. Huge chunk of iceberg visible — labelled 'SCARED, LONELY, TIRED, CONFUSED.' VOICE: '...but this is what's actually there.' CUT TO: A child looking at their own iceberg drawing, nodding slowly. VOICE: 'When you know what's really there, you can actually do something with it.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The iceberg is brilliantly visual for this age. Make it physical — large printed icebergs with a clear water line. The 'Inside Out' reference will resonate strongly with this generation. Reassure children that the below-water part is for them — they don't have to share.

Core Concept: Sometimes things happen that make us feel sad, scared, or hurt — and even when those things are over, we might still feel them inside. Today we talk about those feelings in a gentle, safe way, and remember that carrying something hard doesn't mean we're stuck with it forever.
Opening Hook: Has anyone ever had a bad day, or a bad thing happen, and it kept making you feel yucky even after it was over? That's completely normal. Today we talk about that.
Signal Metaphor: Imagine you found a heavy stone and put it in your pocket. You might forget it's there after a while — but it's still making everything a little harder. Sometimes our feelings are like that. Today we look at the stones we might be carrying and decide which ones we can put down.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories the bravest characters were never the ones with no fears or no hurts. They were the ones who knew about their fears — and went anyway. Bravery is not the absence of hurt. Bravery is carrying what's real and continuing forward.
Teaching Points: 1. Hard things happen to everyone — that's part of being human. | 2. When something hard happens, sometimes the feeling doesn't go away straight away. It might stay in your tummy or make you feel quiet or sad for a while. | 3. That's okay. Those feelings are telling you the hard thing mattered — and that you mattered. | 4. We don't have to carry all the hard things alone. That's what trusted grown-ups, friends, and places like this are for.
Experiential Exercise: THE STONE ACTIVITY: Everyone gets a smooth stone (or draws a stone on paper). On one side: draw or write something hard that happened — something you're still carrying a little bit. Facilitator shares their own gentle example first. On the other side: draw or write one person, place, or thing that helps you feel better when things are hard. Share the 'helper' side with the group. 'This stone represents your hard thing AND your helper. You carry both.'
Guided Reflection: Hold your stone or put your hand on your drawing. Close your eyes. Think about something that was hard. Now imagine all the people who care about you — family, friends, teachers — standing around you. You're not carrying this alone. That's important to know.
Journaling Prompt: Draw or write about a grown-up or friend you would go to if you were carrying something heavy. What makes them safe to talk to?
Weekly Practice (Mon): If your stone feels heavy today, talk to a grown-up you trust about what's making it heavy.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Show a grown-up your stone drawing and explain what the two sides mean.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring your stone (or stone drawing) back. Has anything gotten easier to carry since last week?
Core Affirmation: Hard things happen. But I don't carry them alone — and they don't get to be the whole story.
Video Description: YouTube: 'The Invisible String' read-aloud — a beautiful story about connection that remains even through difficult times. Runtime ~8 min. Companion book: 'A Little Spot of Sadness' by Diane Alber — child-friendly approach to grief and loss.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A child walking with a heavy backpack. With each step, it looks heavier. VOICE: 'Sometimes we carry hard things for a long time without telling anyone.' CUT TO: The child stops. Looks at the backpack. VOICE: 'You don't have to carry it alone.' CUT TO: Another person joins them — walking beside them. The backpack looks the same, but the child's face is different. Lighter. VOICE: 'Telling someone about the heavy thing doesn't make it disappear. But it does mean you have company.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: CRITICAL: Most emotionally sensitive children's session. Do NOT ask children to share what is in their 'stone' unless they choose to. Have a quiet space available. Coordinate with parents/caregivers before this session and provide a resource sheet for families. Have the children's programme lead available if any disclosures are made.

Session Title: The Real Face and the Pretend Faces
Core Concept: Sometimes we act differently around different people — maybe you're super silly with your best friend but quieter at school. Sometimes that's fine! But sometimes we hide the real us because we're worried people won't like us. Today we talk about feeling safe enough to be yourself.
Opening Hook: Let's play a game! Can you show me your 'at school' face? Your 'at home' face? Your 'playing with best friends' face? Your 'feeling shy' face? Now — can you show me your REAL face? What makes that one different?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine you have a special face — your real face — and then you also have some pretend faces you wear when you're not sure if it's safe to be yourself. Today we talk about the real face, and when it's safe to show it.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories the greatest friendships and the greatest adventures always started with someone being brave enough to be real — to say 'this is who I actually am.' The friends who matter always want to know the real you. Today we practise being real.
Teaching Points: 1. Everyone acts a little differently in different places — that's totally normal. | 2. Sometimes we wear a pretend face because we're not sure if people will like our real face. | 3. But wearing pretend faces all the time gets tiring — and it means people can't really know you. | 4. Being yourself takes bravery. But the right people — the ones who really matter — will like your real face best.
Experiential Exercise: MASK MAKING ACTIVITY: Each child gets a paper mask template to colour and decorate as a 'pretend face' they sometimes wear (e.g. 'the brave face,' 'the happy face when I'm not happy,' 'the cool face'). On the BACK of the mask, they write or draw their real feelings or qualities. Share: 'My pretend face looks like... but on the back, I'm really...'
Guided Reflection: Hold your mask up. Now lower it slowly. Imagine the people who love you most — your favourite people in the world — are looking at your real face. Does it feel okay? Scary? Warm? The right people think your real face is the best face.
Journaling Prompt: Draw two faces: your pretend face for one situation, and your real face underneath. What's the same? What's different?
Weekly Practice (Mon): Notice once today when you're wearing a pretend face. You don't have to change it — just notice it's there.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Show a grown-up your mask craft. Tell them about one pretend face you wear and one time you felt safe to be your real self.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring your mask back! Has anything been different this week about showing your real face?
Core Affirmation: My real face is the best face. The right people will always want to see it.
Video Description: YouTube: 'The Name Jar' read-aloud — story about a child who hides their real name and finds the courage to claim it. Runtime ~8 min. Companion book: 'Stand Tall, Molly Lou Melon' by Patty Lovell — a small girl who is completely herself despite pressure to change.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A child holding up a beautiful painted mask. Bright colours. Perfect. VOICE: 'It's a beautiful mask. Everyone thinks so.' CUT TO: The same child lowering the mask. Their real face — more interesting, more alive, a bit uncertain. VOICE: 'But look at THIS face.' CUT TO: Best friend, seeing the real face. Grinning. VOICE: 'The right people always prefer the real one.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The mask craft is one of the most enjoyable physical activities of Phase 1 — have good craft supplies available. The two-sided mask (performance on front, real self on back) is a powerful metaphor children can take home. Coordinate with families — the mask can prompt great conversations at home.

Core Concept: Sometimes we think we know exactly why someone did something — but we might be wrong! Today we practise the superpower of seeing things from other people's point of view, which is one of the kindest and most useful things you can learn to do.
Opening Hook: Let's try something: (Facilitator holds up a duck/rabbit optical illusion.) What do you see? Does anyone see something different? Both are right! That's what today is about.
Signal Metaphor: Imagine you're looking at a picture of a dog and your friend is looking at it from the other side of the room — and they say 'it's a cat!' You might think they're wrong. But what if they can see a different part of the picture from where they're standing? Today we practise walking around to see what other people see.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories the wisest characters always had the ability to see things from many sides — like a jewel that shimmers differently depending on which angle you hold it at. That wisdom — the ability to really try to understand how things look to someone else — is a skill anyone can learn.
Teaching Points: 1. Everyone sees the world from where THEY'RE standing — based on their experiences, feelings, and what's happened to them. | 2. Sometimes when someone does something that seems unkind, there might be something happening for them that we don't know about. | 3. Trying to imagine how things look from someone else's place is called empathy — and it's one of the most important things you can learn. | 4. It doesn't mean you have to agree with them or let them be unkind to you. It just helps you understand — and understanding usually leads to kinder choices.
Experiential Exercise: THE PERSPECTIVE DETECTIVE: Facilitator presents three short scenarios (e.g. 'Tom took Maya's pencil without asking. Maya is upset. But Tom forgot his pencils today and has a big test.'). For each: how might each person be feeling? What might each person be thinking? Is there a kind way to understand both sides? Then: think of a real situation where someone did something that confused or upset you. What might THEIR side of the story be?
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think of a time someone did something that upset or confused you. Now imagine you can magically see inside their head for a moment — what might have been going on for them? Were they maybe scared, tired, sad, or confused themselves? Does it make you feel any different about what happened?
Journaling Prompt: Draw a picture of a time something seemed unfair. Then draw what it might have looked like from the other person's point of view.
Weekly Practice (Mon): Once today when someone does something confusing, ask yourself: 'I wonder what's going on for THEM right now?'
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about a time you tried to see things from someone else's point of view this week.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back a story about a time you tried to be a 'perspective detective' this week!
Core Affirmation: I can try to see how things look from where someone else is standing. That's how I grow kinder.
Video Description: YouTube: 'We're All Wonders' read-aloud by R.J. Palacio — companion to 'Wonder,' the gold standard for teaching children empathy. Runtime ~5 min. Full book 'Wonder' also highly recommended.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: Two cartoon kids looking at the same picture from opposite sides. From one side it looks like a duck. From the other, a rabbit. VOICE: 'Are they both right? Or both wrong?' CUT TO: Each child walks around to where the other is standing. Eyes widen. VOICE: 'Both right. Just from different places.' CUT TO: The two kids looking at the picture together, both seeing both animals. VOICE: 'That's what perspective is. And it makes you better at being a friend.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: Use physical props — perspective illusions work brilliantly for this age. The duck/rabbit or young woman/old woman illusion is classic and always provokes delight. The perspective detective game should be kept fun and curious, not moralistic.

Weekly Theme: The Habit Loop — How We Got Here
Core Concept: A habit is something we do so often that we start doing it without even thinking! Some habits are really good — like brushing teeth. Some habits might not help us as much. Today we look at habits and figure out how they work.
Opening Hook: Let's make a list together: what are some habits that HELP us? (Brushing teeth, saying please, getting enough sleep.) What are some habits that might NOT help as much? Which ones did you decide? Which ones just... happened?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine there's a little path in a garden. The first time someone walks it, they have to push through the grass. The tenth time, the grass is worn down. The hundredth time — there's a clear path. Habits are like that path. The more you walk them, the more automatic they become.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In many old traditions, teachers would ask students: 'What do you do without thinking?' Not to criticise — but to help them see what had become automatic. Seeing what we do automatically is the beginning of being able to choose. And choice is a superpower.
Teaching Points: 1. A habit is anything we do so often that our brain does it automatically — without us needing to think about it. | 2. Habits have three parts: TRIGGER (what starts it), ACTION (what we do), and REWARD (what we get). | 3. When something is a habit, the brain saves energy by doing it automatically. That's great for useful habits! | 4. We can change habits — but we need to understand how they work first. And the first step is just NOTICING them.
Experiential Exercise: THE HABIT DETECTIVE GAME: Facilitator walks through the habit loop using a fun example (e.g. 'Whenever I see the biscuit tin — TRIGGER — I open it and take one — ACTION — and it tastes yummy — REWARD'). Children brainstorm their own habits — good and less helpful. For each habit: what's the TRIGGER? What's the ACTION? What's the REWARD? Then: 'Could we change the ACTION while keeping the same REWARD? What could we do instead?'
Guided Reflection: Think of one habit you have. Close your eyes and trace it: what usually happens just before you do it (the trigger)? What do you actually do (the action)? How do you feel right after (the reward)? Now: is this a habit you want to keep, change, or build more of?
Journaling Prompt: Draw your habit loop: trigger → action → reward. Then draw what a NEW action could look like that still gets the same reward!
Weekly Practice (Mon): Today, catch one habit as it's about to happen. You don't have to change it — just notice the trigger and say 'ah, there it is!'
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about one habit you noticed this week. What was the trigger? What was the reward?
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back your habit loop drawing AND a story about one habit you noticed!
Core Affirmation: I notice my habits. Noticing them means I can choose what I want to do next.
Video Description: YouTube: 'The Power of Yet' — Carol Dweck animated for kids, about the habit of giving up vs. the habit of persisting. Runtime ~5 min. Companion book: 'The Bad Seed' by Jory John — hilarious story about a seed who always did things one way and decides to change.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: Cartoon path forming in grass — each footstep more defined. VOICE: 'Every time you do something, you're walking a path in your brain.' CUT TO: A well-worn path. Deep and automatic. VOICE: 'Some paths are really helpful! Some... not so much.' CUT TO: Cartoon child choosing to step off the old path. First steps through longer grass — a little harder. VOICE: 'Making a new path takes a little more effort at first. But the more you walk it...' CUT TO: New path forming, becoming clear. VOICE: '...the easier it gets.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The three-part habit loop is perfectly age-appropriate for primary school children. Use physical role-play for the habit detective game — act it out with the whole group. Send a 'habit detective worksheet' home for family engagement.

Core Concept: We've been on a big adventure together for 13 weeks — looking at feelings, habits, patterns, and all sorts of things about ourselves. Today we celebrate how brave we've been, and get ready for the next exciting part of the journey.
Opening Hook: Let's go on a memory adventure! What are all the things we've learned about ourselves over the past 13 weeks? (Let children call out — signals and noise, the pause button, the gremlin, habit detective, feelings iceberg, perspective detective...)
Signal Metaphor: Remember at the start of our adventure, we collected tools: the pause button, the feelings radar, the gremlin's name, the habit detective badge. Today we take everything out, look at all the tools we've collected, and celebrate how full our backpacks have become.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In every great adventure story there's a moment where the hero looks back at how far they've come before heading towards the next challenge. They don't usually feel completely different — but they have tools they didn't have before. Today is that moment.
Teaching Points: 1. You've been incredibly brave over the past 13 weeks — looking at your feelings, habits, inner voice, and how you see the world. | 2. All the tools we've collected are yours to keep — forever. You can use them any time. | 3. Growing is not about being perfect. It's about noticing more, understanding better, and being a little kinder to yourself. | 4. Phase 2 of our adventure is about something really exciting: choosing which old things we want to carry differently — and building new things.
Experiential Exercise: BACKPACK CELEBRATION: Each child gets a backpack outline and draws all the 'tools' they've collected over 13 weeks. Decorate the backpack with favourite colours, patterns, anything that feels like 'them.' Circle time: each child shares ONE favourite tool from the journey so far. Celebrate each share genuinely and specifically.
Guided Reflection: Hold your backpack drawing. Close your eyes. Think about the very first day we met. Did you know any of these tools then? Now think about all the times you've used them or tried to. You are braver than you were. You know yourself a little better. That's something to be really proud of.
Journaling Prompt: Draw what your 'inner self' looks like now compared to Week 1. What has changed? What has stayed the same?
Weekly Practice (Mon): Share your backpack with someone at home — tell them about every tool in it!
Weekly Practice (Wed): Show a grown-up your Phase 1 drawings and tell them your favourite thing you learned about yourself.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Come to the next session ready to show your backpack and share your FAVOURITE thing from Phase 1!
Core Affirmation: I have new tools. I am braver than I was. And the adventure is just beginning.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'growth mindset celebration kids' for an affirming short animation to celebrate learning and bravery. Runtime ~3–5 min. Companion book: 'Last Stop on Market Street' by Matt de la Pena — about seeing what you have and where you're going.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A backpack, at first empty. Then over a montage, tools fill it one by one — the pause button, the feelings map, the gremlin drawing, the habit loop, the mirror craft. VOICE: 'Look at everything you've collected.' CUT TO: Child shouldering the full backpack — lighter than expected. Smiling. VOICE: 'The backpack full of self-knowledge is the lightest one there is.' CUT TO: Child at a crossroads, looking forward. VOICE: 'Phase 2 begins now. And you're ready.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE — Phase 2: Unlearn.
Facilitator Notes: Make this session genuinely celebratory — balloons, music, certificates if you have them. Children deserve to have their work honoured. Put all backpack drawings up around the room together — creates genuine community pride. Phase 2 transition should feel exciting and earned.

Weekly Theme: The Permission You're Still Waiting For
Core Concept: Sometimes we don't try things because we're waiting for someone to say it's okay. But some of the best, most YOU things you could do — you already have permission for. Today we find out what you've been waiting to try.
Opening Hook: Has anyone ever had an idea or wanted to try something new — but didn't, because they weren't sure if they were allowed? What was it?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine there's a big green GO button inside you. Sometimes we forget it's there and keep looking around for someone else to press it for us. Today we practise pressing our own GO button.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: There's an old story about a small bird who refused to fly because nobody had ever told it that it could. One day it fell off a branch — and discovered it had been able to fly all along. You have abilities and ideas waiting for you to discover them. Today we practise leaping.
Teaching Points: 1. It's always good to check with trusted adults before doing new things — that's smart, not weak. | 2. But some things — like trying a new creative idea, being kind in a new way, or deciding what you enjoy — you already have permission for. | 3. Sometimes we wait when we don't need to wait. And that means missing out on things that belong to us. | 4. Today we practise asking ourselves first: 'Is this something I can just... try?'
Experiential Exercise: THE GO BUTTON GAME: Facilitator presents scenarios: 'You have an idea for a story. Do you need permission to write it? GO or WAIT?' / 'You want to try a new sport. WAIT — ask a grown-up.' / 'You want to be kinder to someone who isn't your friend. GO?' Play through 6–8 scenarios, getting children to identify which decisions are theirs and which need adult input. Then: 'What's one thing YOU have been waiting to try that you actually have permission for right now?'
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think of one thing you've been wanting to try or do. Now ask yourself: 'Do I actually need permission for this? Or do I already have it?' If you already have it — what would you do first?
Journaling Prompt: Draw your GO button. What does it look like? What would you press it to do first?
Weekly Practice (Mon): Try one small thing today that you've been waiting to try. It doesn't have to be big — just something that's yours to try.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about your GO button. Ask them: 'What's something you wish you'd given yourself permission to try sooner?'
Weekly Practice (Sun): Come back with a story about one thing you pressed your GO button on this week!
Core Affirmation: I have permission to try, to create, to be curious. That permission lives inside me.
Video Description: YouTube: 'What Do You Do With an Idea?' read-aloud by Kobi Yamada — a child learns to trust and act on their own idea despite uncertainty. Runtime ~8 min.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A child standing at the edge of a diving board — looking down. Nervous. Other children swimming below, calling up. VOICE: 'Sometimes the only thing holding us back... is waiting for someone to say it's okay.' CUT TO: The child takes a breath. Looks down. Jumps. CUT TO: Surfacing. Laughing. VOICE: 'Some GO buttons, only you can press.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The GO/WAIT game is highly engaging and teaches important discernment — not all things are children's decisions, and that's appropriate to name. Celebrate any share about something they pressed GO on. Keep it playful and empowering.

Weekly Theme: Letting Go of Who You Were Supposed to Be
Core Concept: Sometimes grown-ups and other people have ideas about what we should be when we grow up, or how we should act, or what we should like. Those ideas come from love — but sometimes they're not exactly right for us. Today we explore what WE actually love and who WE actually are.
Opening Hook: What do you love doing that feels most like YOU — not because someone told you to love it, but because you just do?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine a colouring book where someone has already drawn the outlines and chosen the colours. That can be nice! But what if YOU want to draw your own picture from scratch? Today we think about which parts of your 'picture' came from other people — and which parts are completely, originally yours.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, the most interesting characters were never the ones who followed someone else's map exactly. They were the ones who made their own path — sometimes scary, always more truly theirs. Today we start drawing our own map.
Teaching Points: 1. There are things we love and things we're good at that belong completely to us. | 2. Sometimes people who love us have ideas about what we should like or who we should be — and those ideas come from love, even if they're not always right. | 3. It's okay to enjoy things people didn't expect you to enjoy. It's okay to be different from what anyone planned. | 4. The most important question is always: does this feel like ME?
Experiential Exercise: MY OWN PICTURE: Each child gets a blank piece of paper (not a colouring-in page — a completely blank one). 'Draw or write things that feel most like you — what you love, what you're curious about, what you dream about, what makes you feel most alive.' No templates. No outlines. Completely theirs. Share: 'One thing in my picture that might surprise people who think they know me.'
Guided Reflection: Look at your picture. Close your eyes. Think: if nobody ever told you what to be or what to like, is this still what you'd choose? How does it feel to know that this — this real, specific, particular you — is already here?
Journaling Prompt: Write or draw about something you love that feels completely, uniquely yours — maybe something not everyone understands.
Weekly Practice (Mon): Today, do one thing just because YOU love it — not because anyone told you to.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Show a grown-up your 'My Own Picture' drawing. Tell them one thing about yourself they might not know.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring your 'My Own Picture' back and add something new you discovered about yourself this week!
Core Affirmation: Who I am is already here. I get to discover it — and it belongs to me.
Video Description: YouTube: 'What Do You Do With an Idea?' read-aloud by Kobi Yamada — about nurturing the things that belong most deeply to you. Runtime ~8 min. Companion book: 'The Dot' by Peter Reynolds — about the courage to make your own mark.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A blank piece of paper on a desk. Pencil hovering. VOICE: 'Before anyone told you what to draw... what would you have put here?' CUT TO: A child beginning to draw — tentatively at first, then with growing confidence. Something entirely their own. VOICE: 'That thing. Right there. That's yours.' CUT TO: Finished drawing. Completely original. Completely them. VOICE: 'Don't let anyone else fill in your blank page.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The blank page exercise is deliberately unstructured — resist the urge to add prompts or templates. The blankness is the point. Celebrate every drawing as completely valid. This session plants a seed about intrinsic identity that will deepen throughout the year.

Core Concept: Sometimes people hurt our feelings or do things that aren't fair — and it can be really hard to stop feeling angry or sad about it. Today we talk about something called forgiveness — what it really means, and how it can help US feel better.
Opening Hook: Has anyone ever felt really angry or sad about something someone did — and kept thinking about it even when you didn't want to? What does that feel like?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine you're holding a really hot rock that someone threw at you. It burned your hand and it wasn't fair. But you're STILL holding it — and it's still hurting you. Forgiving someone is like putting the hot rock down. Not saying the throw was okay. Just putting the rock down so your hand can heal.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, the characters who could forgive — not forget, but forgive — were always the strongest ones. Because letting go of a heavy thing takes more courage than holding on to it.
Teaching Points: 1. When someone hurts us it's completely normal to feel angry or sad — those feelings are real and valid. | 2. Forgiveness doesn't mean what happened was okay. It doesn't mean you have to be friends with the person again. | 3. Forgiveness means choosing to stop carrying the heavy hurt around — so that YOU can feel better. | 4. It's okay if forgiveness takes time. It usually does. Today we just start thinking about it.
Experiential Exercise: THE HOT ROCK ACTIVITY: Each child gets a smooth stone. On it they write (or the facilitator helps write) something that happened that hurt them — a time someone was unkind. Then: hold the stone tight in your fist. Feel how heavy it is. How it doesn't feel nice to keep squeezing it. Now slowly open your hand and just... rest it there. You're not throwing it away. You're just stopping squeezing. Discuss: what's the difference between holding tight and just resting it in your open hand?
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes and imagine the thing that hurt you. Notice where you feel it in your body. Now imagine slowly opening your hand and letting the stone just rest there — not throwing it away, not pretending it didn't happen, just not squeezing anymore. Does anything feel different?
Journaling Prompt: Draw a picture of you holding the hot rock. Then draw a picture of you with your hand open, the rock resting in it. What's different about your face?
Weekly Practice (Mon): When you think about something that hurt you today, try opening your fist instead of squeezing it tighter.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a trusted grown-up about something you're still feeling hurt about. Ask them to help you think about it.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back: did you try opening your hand this week? What happened?
Core Affirmation: I can put down heavy things. Letting go is one of the bravest things I can do.
Video Description: YouTube: 'Each Kindness' by Jacqueline Woodson read-aloud — about the weight of things left unresolved and the power of choosing differently. Runtime ~8 min. Companion book: 'Enemy Pie' by Derek Munson — about releasing a grievance and discovering friendship.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A cartoon child's hand, tightly fisted around a glowing red rock. Their whole body tense. VOICE: 'That rock — it wasn't theirs to give you. But you've been holding it ever since.' CUT TO: Slowly, the fist opens. The rock is still there — but no longer being squeezed. The glow fades slightly. The child's face softens. VOICE: 'Putting it down doesn't mean it didn't happen. It just means you don't have to keep carrying the heat.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The hot rock exercise is highly physical and effective for this age. Ensure children understand clearly: forgiveness is not saying the hurt was okay, and it doesn't mean having to be friends with the person. Have a check-in with parents after this session if any significant hurts are disclosed.

Core Concept: Sometimes we do things we feel really bad about — maybe we said something unkind or made a mistake that hurt someone. It's good to feel sorry. But today we learn that after we've said sorry and tried to make it right, we don't need to keep feeling bad forever.
Opening Hook: Has anyone ever done something by accident or on purpose that they felt really bad about? What did it feel like? Did you say sorry? And did you feel better afterwards — or did the bad feeling stay for a long time?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine you accidentally knocked over your friend's drink. You felt terrible. You said sorry. You helped clean it up. Now imagine still feeling terrible about it three weeks later. That wouldn't be helpful anymore, would it? Today we learn how to say sorry properly — and then let ourselves feel okay again.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, characters who made mistakes had a choice: they could spend the whole story feeling terrible and not trying again — or they could learn, make it right, and keep going. The brave ones always chose to keep going.
Teaching Points: 1. When we do something that hurts someone — even by accident — it's normal to feel sad or sorry. That feeling is called guilt, and it's actually a sign that you care about doing what's right. | 2. The right steps are: acknowledge what happened, say sorry properly, try to make it right if you can. | 3. After you've done those things, you don't need to keep punishing yourself. You're allowed to feel okay again. | 4. We all make mistakes. All of us. Even grown-ups. Making mistakes doesn't make you bad — it makes you human.
Experiential Exercise: THE SORRY STEPS: Teach the four steps on a poster or card: 1. SAY WHAT HAPPENED (no excuses). 2. SAY SORRY and mean it. 3. MAKE IT RIGHT if you can (what can you do?). 4. LEARN and do better next time. Role-play scenarios together. Then: think of something you still feel bad about. Have you done all four steps? If yes — you have permission to let the bad feeling go. If not — which step is still needed?
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think of something you still feel a little bad about. Have you said sorry? Have you tried to make it right? If yes — imagine a kind voice saying to you: 'You did the right things. You don't need to carry this anymore. You're a good person who made a mistake. That's different from being bad.' How does that feel?
Journaling Prompt: Draw the four sorry steps as a little comic strip. When would you use them?
Weekly Practice (Mon): If you still feel bad about something today, work through the four steps. What still needs to be done?
Weekly Practice (Wed): Show a grown-up the four sorry steps. Ask them about a time they had to forgive themselves for something.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back: did you use the four sorry steps this week? What happened?
Core Affirmation: I can make mistakes and still be a good person. I say sorry, I make it right, and I keep going.
Video Description: YouTube: 'The Invisible String' or search 'sorry steps for kids animated' — various short animations on apology and self-forgiveness for young children. Runtime ~5 min. Companion book: 'Sorry!' by Trudy Ludwig — a story about what a real apology looks and feels like.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A cartoon child with a big grey cloud over their head — carrying guilt. VOICE: 'The cloud showed up when something went wrong. And it's been there ever since.' CUT TO: The child says sorry. Tries to make it right. Learns something. VOICE: 'Those four steps — those are all you need.' CUT TO: The cloud begins to lift. Not disappear — lift. The child can see the sky again. VOICE: 'You're not bad. You made a mistake. Those are different things.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: Ensure the four-step process is concrete and memorable — put it on a card they can take home. Distinguish clearly between guilt (healthy, processable) and shame (unhealthy, prolonged). The goal is not to minimise accountability but to show children how to complete the cycle.

Weekly Theme: Rewiring the Critic — Building the Inner Coach
Core Concept: Remember the gremlin from a few weeks ago? Today we give more power to the OTHER voice — the kind, honest, encouraging one. We're going to build our own inner coach — a voice that's on our side AND tells us the truth.
Opening Hook: Think about a coach, teacher, or grown-up who really believed in you. What did they say? How did it feel different from when someone was just mean or critical?
Signal Metaphor: The gremlin says mean things. But remember — there's another voice too. A coach voice. Coaches push you to get better AND they believe in you at the same time. Today we practise making that voice louder.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In stories about heroes, there's always a wise guide — someone who believes in the hero even when the hero doesn't believe in themselves. Gandalf. Dumbledore. The cricket from Pinocchio. Today we practise becoming that wise guide for ourselves.
Teaching Points: 1. We all have different voices in our head — the gremlin voice (mean and not helpful), and the coach voice (honest AND kind). | 2. A good coach tells you the truth — but they also believe you can do it. | 3. The more we practise the coach voice, the louder it gets. It's like a muscle — the more you use it, the stronger it becomes. | 4. Today we practise what our inner coach sounds like.
Experiential Exercise: THE COACH VS. GREMLIN GAME: Facilitator presents scenarios and groups decide: gremlin or coach? 'You'll never get this right' vs. 'That was tricky — let's try it a different way.' 'You're so embarrassing' vs. 'That felt awkward, but you were brave to try.' 'Nobody wants to play with you' vs. 'Making friends can be hard — who could you start with?' Then: for your own gremlin's favourite line, write or draw what YOUR coach would say instead. Share your coach line with the group.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think of something you find hard. Hear the gremlin say something about it. Now — imagine your coach stepping in. What does your coach say? How does that feel different? Which voice do you want to get louder?
Journaling Prompt: Draw your inner coach. What do they look like? What is their name? What is their most important saying?
Weekly Practice (Mon): When the gremlin speaks today, try having your coach answer back. Even quietly.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Introduce your inner coach to a grown-up. Tell them the coach's name and what they say.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring your inner coach drawing back! Did they help you this week?
Core Affirmation: My inner coach is kind AND honest. The more I listen, the louder they get.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'inner coach for kids animated' or 'positive self-talk for children' for short accessible animations. Runtime ~5 min. Companion book: 'The Girl Who Never Made Mistakes' by Mark Pett — about learning to be your own kind witness.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: Split screen — the gremlin whispering on one shoulder, the coach on the other. VOICE: 'They've both been there all along. The question is who gets the microphone.' CUT TO: The child practising the coach's voice. Quietly at first. VOICE: 'The coach voice gets stronger every time you use it. Just like a muscle.' CUT TO: The child in a tough moment — coach voice louder now. Managing it differently. VOICE: 'That's the work. That's the whole thing.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: Children love creating and naming their inner coach — it becomes a long-running character they can reference throughout the year. Display coach drawings alongside gremlin drawings from Week 7 — the visual comparison is powerful. Coordinate with parents so they can reinforce the coach language at home.

Core Concept: Sometimes we do things we don't really want to do, or say we're okay when we're not, just so other people feel happy. That's called people-pleasing — and while it feels kind, it can actually stop us from being honest and taking care of ourselves. Today we learn the difference between being kind and trying to make everyone happy all the time.
Opening Hook: Has anyone ever done something they didn't really want to do just so someone else wouldn't be upset? What did that feel like?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine you have a cup of energy. Every time you do something kind because you genuinely want to, the cup stays full. But every time you do something just so someone won't be upset with you — even when you don't want to — the cup gets a little emptier. Today we learn to tell the difference.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, the characters who tried to make everyone happy all the time usually ended up in trouble — because they kept saying yes when they meant no, until everything got very confusing. The characters who were honest — even when it was uncomfortable — those were usually the ones things worked out for.
Teaching Points: 1. Being kind means genuinely caring about other people — and that's wonderful. | 2. People-pleasing is different — it means saying yes or pretending to be okay even when you're not, because you're worried about what someone will think or feel. | 3. It's okay for other people to feel disappointed sometimes. That's part of life. | 4. Learning to be honest — even when it's a little uncomfortable — is one of the kindest things you can do, because people get to know the real you.
Experiential Exercise: KIND or PEOPLE-PLEASING? Play through scenarios: 'Your friend wants to play a game you find boring. You play anyway because you love them and it will make them happy.' (KIND — genuine choice.) 'Someone asks if you like their drawing. You say yes even though you don't, because you're scared they'll be upset.' (PEOPLE-PLEASING.) 'You don't want to go to the party but say you do because you're worried everyone will be mad at you.' (PEOPLE-PLEASING.) Discuss: what's the difference? How can you tell from the inside? What does each one feel like in your body?
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think of a time you said yes when you meant no. How did your body feel while you were saying it? And after? Now think of a time you were genuinely kind — something you wanted to do. How did THAT feel? Can you feel the difference?
Journaling Prompt: Draw a picture showing the difference between being kind (from the heart) and people-pleasing (from fear).
Weekly Practice (Mon): Today, notice if you do something just to make someone happy rather than because you genuinely want to. You don't have to change it — just notice.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about the difference between being kind and people-pleasing. Ask them if they ever do it too.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back: did you notice a people-pleasing moment this week? What happened?
Core Affirmation: I can be kind AND honest. I don't need to pretend to take care of myself.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'saying no for kids read aloud' or 'personal boundaries for children' for short accessible animations. Runtime ~5 min. Companion book: 'My Body Belongs to Me' by Jill Starishevsky — extends into body boundaries and personal authority.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A cartoon child saying yes, yes, yes — each yes making them a little more tired, a little more invisible. VOICE: 'They're so busy making everyone else happy... there's no space left for them.' CUT TO: The child, quietly, trying something different. A gentle, honest 'actually, I don't really want to.' VOICE: 'That was scary. And that was brave. And the world didn't end.' CUT TO: The child — still kind, but more themselves. More present. VOICE: 'Kind and honest. You can be both.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: Keep this session warm and non-shame-based — many children are actively taught to prioritise others' feelings above their own. The goal is discernment, not selfishness. Involve parents by sending home a note about the session so they can reinforce the language.

Session Title: The Things That Don't Run Out
Core Concept: Sometimes we worry that there isn't enough — enough time, enough love, enough things that are good. Today we practise noticing all the things there actually ARE enough of — and how our brains can sometimes trick us into thinking things are scarcer than they are.
Opening Hook: Has anyone ever worried that there wasn't enough of something — like that they didn't have enough friends, or that someone didn't love them enough? What was that like?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine your brain has a 'worry radar' that scans for anything that might run out. Sometimes it's really helpful! But sometimes it finds problems that aren't really there. Today we learn to tell the difference between real worries and radar false alarms.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, there's often a magic pot or a well that never runs out — no matter how much you take, there's always more. That sounds like a fairy tale. But there ARE things in your life that don't run out when you share them. Love. Kindness. Ideas. Laughter. Today we find them.
Teaching Points: 1. Our brains are designed to notice when things might run out — that was useful for our ancestors. | 2. But sometimes our brains get it wrong and tell us things are running out when they're actually fine. | 3. Some things DO run out — like biscuits. Some things DON'T run out — like love, kindness, ideas, and good memories. Sharing them makes more, not less. | 4. Today we practise noticing all the things in our life that ARE enough.
Experiential Exercise: ENOUGH TREASURE HUNT: Children have 5 minutes to write or draw as many things as they can think of in their life that are 'enough' or 'plentiful': 'I have enough...' — people who love me, fun things to do, things I'm good at, ways I'm kind, good memories. Share the lists. Then: facilitator points out that sharing kindness or ideas never made them smaller. Discuss: what happens to love when you give some away? Does it get smaller — or bigger?
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think about all the people who love you. Now imagine giving some of that love to someone else. Does the love in your heart get smaller — or does it stay the same? What about kind thoughts? Ideas? Smiles? Some things grow when you share them.
Journaling Prompt: Draw a picture of all the things in your life that there is ENOUGH of. Make it as full as you can!
Weekly Practice (Mon): Today, share one kind thing with someone — and notice if it made your kindness smaller or bigger.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about one thing in your life that you have plenty of. Ask them what they feel they have plenty of too.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back your 'enough' drawing and add three more things you noticed this week!
Core Affirmation: I have enough love, enough kindness, and enough good things in my life. And sharing them makes more.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'The Giving Tree read aloud Shel Silverstein' — a classic story about generosity and what replenishes vs. what depletes. Runtime ~8 min. Also: 'Have You Filled a Bucket Today?' read-aloud — about how kindness replenishes rather than depletes.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A child's worry about having enough — visualised as a shrinking jar. VOICE: 'Sometimes our brains tell us the jar is running out.' CUT TO: The child shares something kind with a friend. Waits. Looks at the jar. VOICE: 'But look. The jar didn't get smaller. It got bigger.' CUT TO: Jar overflowing with colour and light. VOICE: 'Some things you can't run out of when you share them.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The concept of non-depletable resources (love, kindness, ideas) vs. depletable resources (biscuits, time) is a wonderful distinction for this age. Make it concrete and playful. The 'bucket filling' concept from the book is a year-round reference tool — consider making it a classroom/programme resource.

Core Concept: All the people in our lives — family, friends, teachers — teach us things about what being close to someone feels like. Some of those things are wonderful. Some might be a little confusing or hard. Today we think about the people who have shaped us most — and what we want to carry with us.
Opening Hook: Who is one person in your life (or who WAS in your life) who made you feel really safe and loved? What did they teach you about what it feels like to be cared for?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine all the people who've been important to you have each given you a little gift — something you learned from being close to them. Some gifts are beautiful and you want to keep them forever. Some gifts might be a bit confusing and you're not sure they're actually for you. Today we look at the gifts.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories there are always the wise elders — people whose influence stays with the hero long after they've parted. The hero carries what was good and leaves behind what wasn't theirs to carry. Today we think about who has been our wise elder — and what they gave us.
Teaching Points: 1. All the important people in our lives teach us something about what being close to someone feels like. | 2. Some of what we learn is wonderful — how to trust, how to feel loved, how to be kind. | 3. Some of what we learn might be confusing — maybe some relationships made us feel unsure or worried. | 4. We get to look at all of it and decide: what do I want to keep? What do I want to do differently?
Experiential Exercise: THE RELATIONSHIP GIFTS BOX: Each child draws a gift box. Inside the box, they draw or write gifts from important relationships — 'from [name] I learned...' Keep it positive focus: what good things did they learn? Around the outside of the box, draw or write: 'I also want to learn more about...' (i.e. things they wish their relationships had taught them). Share: one gift from inside your box.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think of someone who taught you what it feels like to be truly loved and safe. How does it feel to remember them? Now think: what's one thing you learned from them that you want to take with you forever?
Journaling Prompt: Draw a person who has shaped you and write three things you learned from being in a relationship with them.
Weekly Practice (Mon): Today, thank someone (in person, in a letter, or in your heart) for something they gave you.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about one thing they've taught you that you want to carry with you. Watch their face.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back your gift box drawing and tell us about the best gift inside it!
Core Affirmation: The people who love me teach me things I carry forever. I choose the gifts I keep.
Video Description: YouTube: 'Wonder' read-aloud clips or 'Wilfred Gordon McDonald Partridge' read-aloud — a beautiful story about what we carry from relationships and what we give to others. Runtime ~8 min.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A child's hands, holding various small objects — each one representing something learned from a relationship. Some bright, some dull. VOICE: 'Everyone who's been close to you has left something.' CUT TO: The child carefully choosing which ones to put in their pocket. Holding each one up to the light. VOICE: 'You don't have to keep everything that was given to you. Some things were never yours to carry.' CUT TO: Child walking forward, pockets full of the bright ones. Lighter. VOICE: 'You get to choose.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: Keep this session positive and boundaried — focus on what was given rather than what was withheld or damaged. Children who have experienced significant relational harm need professional support, not a group session. If something concerning is disclosed, follow your duty of care protocol and refer to appropriate support.

Core Concept: Sometimes when we've been hurt before, we build a little protective wall around our heart — we might not share our real feelings, or we might try to look like nothing bothers us. Today we talk about why those walls go up, what they do, and when it might be safe to put a door in them.
Opening Hook: Has anyone ever tried to look like something doesn't bother them when it actually does? Or acted tougher than you felt? What's that like?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine you have an invisible shield. It keeps you safe when things feel scary or hurtful. But sometimes the shield is up even when it doesn't need to be — and then it also blocks the nice things. Today we learn when to use our shield and when it's safe to put it down.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, the heroes always had a shield — but the wisest ones knew when to use it and when to set it aside. A shield you never put down stops being protection and starts being a wall. And walls keep out friends as well as danger.
Teaching Points: 1. When something hurts us, our brain builds a little protective shield to stop us getting hurt the same way again. | 2. That's really smart!
