But sometimes the shield stays up even when it's safe to put it down. | 3. When our shield is always up, we can miss out on good things too — like people who want to be close to us, or fun we could be having. | 4. The best shields have doors in them — so we can let the right people in when we're ready.
Experiential Exercise: THE SHIELD WITH A DOOR: Each child draws a shield. On the shield they draw or write what it protects them from (things that feel scary or hurtful). Then they draw a door in the shield. On the door they write: 'I open this for people who...' (e.g. 'keep my secrets,' 'are kind to me,' 'make me feel safe'). Share: what your door needs before you open it.
Guided Reflection: Hold your shield drawing. Close your eyes. Think about a time you had your shield up when you maybe didn't need it. What might have happened if you'd opened the door a little? Was there someone trying to be close to you that you kept out? How does that feel?
Journaling Prompt: Draw your ideal safe person — someone who would deserve to see behind your shield. What makes them trustworthy?
Weekly Practice (Mon): Today, notice if your shield goes up. Ask yourself: is this danger real? Or is the shield just being extra careful?
Weekly Practice (Wed): Show a trusted grown-up your shield drawing. Tell them who you open the door for — and why.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back your shield drawing! Has anything changed about when you use it?
Core Affirmation: I have a shield to keep me safe — and it has a door I can open when I trust someone.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'The Invisible String read aloud' or 'Last Stop on Market Street read aloud' — stories about trust and connection after difficulty. Runtime ~8 min. Book: 'The Rabbit Listened' by Cori Doerrfeld — about allowing someone to be with you in difficulty.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A cartoon child surrounded by an invisible bubble — bouncing everyone gently away. Safe. But also alone. VOICE: 'The bubble works really well. Nothing gets in.' CUT TO: A friend trying to reach through — gently, kindly. VOICE: 'Not even the good stuff.' CUT TO: The child finds a little door in the bubble. Opens it — just a crack. Let's one trusted friend through. VOICE: 'The door doesn't take the bubble away. It just means you get to choose who comes in.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The shield/door metaphor is beautifully concrete for this age. The key message is agency — they control the door. Never push children to lower defences in a group setting. Coordinate with families so they can continue the conversation at home.

Weekly Theme: Grief and Growth — What Endings Make Possible
Core Concept: Sometimes things end or change — friends move away, pets die, families change, things we loved go away. It's completely normal and okay to feel really sad about those things. Today we learn that it's important to let ourselves feel sad — and that after the sadness, something new always becomes possible.
Opening Hook: Has anyone ever lost something or someone that made them really sad? A friend who moved away? A pet who died? Something that changed and you miss? It's okay to talk about those feelings today.
Signal Metaphor: Imagine every ending is like autumn — the leaves fall, everything looks bare and a bit sad. But the tree doesn't die. And the bare branches make space for spring to come. Endings are like autumn. They're not the end of the tree. They're part of the tree's life.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, even the saddest moments always led somewhere. Not immediately. Not easily. But the saddest chapter was never the last chapter. Today we learn to trust that — even when it doesn't feel true yet.
Teaching Points: 1. Feeling sad when something ends is completely normal and healthy — it means you loved something real. | 2. It's important to let yourself feel sad — trying to push the sadness away before it's ready can make it bigger. | 3. But sadness doesn't last forever. Just like autumn leads to winter which leads to spring — feelings change over time. | 4. Talking about your sad feelings, drawing them, or just letting them be there helps them move through.
Experiential Exercise: THE FEELINGS TREE: Each child draws a tree with four sections representing the four seasons. In the autumn section: what is something that has ended or changed that makes you sad? In the winter section: what does that sadness feel like? In the spring section: what small new thing has grown or could grow because of the change? In the summer section: what do you hope the future will bring? Share: your spring section — something small that has grown.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think of something that ended or changed that made you sad. Let yourself feel that sadness for a moment — it's okay, it's safe here. Now: can you think of one tiny good thing that has happened since then? One small spring that came after the autumn? It might be very small. But it's there.
Journaling Prompt: Draw how you feel when something ends. Then draw how you might feel after some time has passed.
Weekly Practice (Mon): If you're feeling sad about something today, find a safe person to tell. You don't have to fix the sadness — just share it.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about something you've felt sad about. Ask them to just listen — you don't need advice, just company.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back your feelings tree! Has anything changed in your spring or summer sections?
Core Affirmation: It's okay to feel sad when things end. Sadness moves through when we let it. And something new always comes.
Video Description: YouTube: 'The Invisible String' read-aloud — a beautiful, gentle story about connection that continues even through endings and loss. Runtime ~8 min. Book: 'The Goodbye Book' by Todd Parr — simple, reassuring, and age-appropriate for all types of loss.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A tree in autumn — leaves falling, everything bare and still. VOICE: 'Autumn looks like the end.' CUT TO: Winter. Quiet. Empty. VOICE: 'Winter looks like nothing is happening.' CUT TO: Spring. One small green bud appearing on a bare branch. VOICE: 'But look.' CUT TO: Summer. Full leaves, warm light, children playing beneath. VOICE: 'The tree never died. It was getting ready.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: This is a sensitive session that may bring up significant losses for some children. Ensure pre-communication with parents/caregivers — particularly if any children in the group have recently experienced bereavement. The seasons metaphor is gentle and non-prescriptive. Maintain access to a pastoral support person.

Weekly Theme: Rewiring Fear — From Threat to Signal
Session Title: The Toast Alarm vs. The Real Fire
Core Concept: Everyone feels scared sometimes — and that's completely okay. Fear is actually really useful when it warns us about real danger. But sometimes our fear alarm goes off when things are just new or a bit uncomfortable — not actually dangerous. Today we learn to tell the difference!
Opening Hook: Can anyone name something that feels scary but isn't actually dangerous? Like talking in front of the class, or trying something new, or meeting someone you don't know? What does scary-but-safe feel like?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine your brain has a fire alarm. Real fires need the alarm! But sometimes the alarm goes off when someone just burns some toast — not a real fire at all. Today we learn which alarms need us to run away, and which ones just need a bit of bravery.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, the bravest heroes weren't the ones who were never scared. They were the ones who felt scared AND kept going anyway. Because they learned that most scary things, once you face them, turn out to be much more manageable than they looked from far away.
Teaching Points: 1. Fear is a brilliant helper — it warns us about real danger so we can stay safe. | 2. But sometimes our fear alarm goes off for things that are just new, uncomfortable, or a bit awkward — not actually dangerous. | 3. Learning to tell the difference is a superpower: 'Is this a REAL fire — or just burnt toast?' | 4. When it's just burnt toast, we can take a breath and be brave. Our body's alarm will calm down once we show it everything is okay.
Experiential Exercise: REAL FIRE or BURNT TOAST? Play through scenarios together: 'A stranger asks you to go somewhere alone' — REAL FIRE (tell a trusted adult). 'You have to do a speech in front of the class' — BURNT TOAST (scary but safe, take a breath). 'Your friends are about to jump off something really high' — REAL FIRE. 'You want to try a new sport but feel nervous' — BURNT TOAST. Then: think of something that feels scary in your life. Real fire or burnt toast? How do you know?
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think of something that feels scary but is probably burnt toast — just new or a bit uncomfortable. Feel the alarm. Now say to yourself: 'This is just burnt toast. I can handle burnt toast.' Take a slow breath. Notice if the alarm quiets down a little.
Journaling Prompt: Draw a burnt toast fear and a real fire fear. How are they different? What do you do for each one?
Weekly Practice (Mon): When you feel your fear alarm today, ask: real fire or burnt toast? Then decide what to do.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about something that's burnt toast for you — scary but safe. Ask them about one of theirs!
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back: did you have a burnt toast moment this week? What happened when you were brave about it?
Core Affirmation: My fear alarm helps keep me safe. And I'm learning when to listen — and when to be brave.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'brave for kids animated fear YouTube' or 'facing fears children animated' for short accessible animations on being courageous about non-dangerous fears. Runtime ~5 min. Book: 'Jabari Jumps' by Gaia Cornwall — a child who is scared to jump off the diving board and works up the courage to try.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A cartoon fire alarm blaring — in a kitchen where someone has burnt toast. VOICE: 'Alarm is on. But is this a real fire?' CUT TO: Child looking around. No fire. Just toast. VOICE: 'Sometimes our brain treats burnt toast the same as a real fire.' CUT TO: Child taking a breath. Opening a window. Alarm quieting. VOICE: 'When you show your brain it's just burnt toast... it calms down. Every time.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The real fire/burnt toast distinction is brilliantly concrete and memorable for this age. Physical breathing practice can be integrated directly into the role-play. This language can become a year-round reference: 'is that a real fire?' Coordinate with parents to use the same language at home.

Weekly Theme: The Stories That No Longer Serve
Core Concept: Sometimes the things we believe about ourselves are a bit out of date — like a picture of you from when you were really little. The picture might have been true then, but it's not the whole picture of you now. Today we look at old stories and think about whether it's time to update them.
Opening Hook: Think of something you used to believe about yourself that might not be as true anymore. Maybe you used to think you couldn't do something — and now you can. What has changed about you?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine a photo album that hasn't been updated for years. It has pictures from when you were a baby, a toddler, a younger kid. Those pictures were true! But they're not the whole story of you. Today we add new pictures — new, updated, more complete pictures of who you actually are now.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, the characters who grew the most were always the ones who were brave enough to see themselves differently — to say 'I am not just the same as I was. I have grown. I have changed. I am more than the old story.' Today we practise that bravery.
Teaching Points: 1. Sometimes we carry old stories about ourselves — things we believed when we were younger — that aren't really true anymore. | 2. Just like you're taller and smarter and more capable than you were a year ago, your story about yourself can grow too. | 3. It takes bravery to update a story — especially if we've been telling it for a long time. | 4. Today we practise noticing what's grown and changed — and adding those things to our story.
Experiential Exercise: THE UPDATED PHOTO ALBUM: Each child gets a four-page 'photo album' template. Page 1: 'An old story I had about myself' (draw or write). Page 2: 'What has changed or grown since then' (draw or write). Page 3: 'Something I can do now that I couldn't do before' (draw or write). Page 4: 'The new updated picture of me' (draw or write — as full and complete as possible). Share: Page 4 — the new updated picture.
Guided Reflection: Hold your photo album. Look at page 1, then page 4. Can you see the journey? The growth? That journey belongs to you — nobody else went on that exact journey. That makes you someone quite remarkable.
Journaling Prompt: Draw 'old you' vs. 'new you' — what has grown and changed? Celebrate every difference!
Weekly Practice (Mon): Today, notice one way you are more than your old story. Tell someone about it.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Show a grown-up your updated photo album. Ask them to tell you one way they have seen you grow.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring your photo album back with a new entry — something that grew this week!
Core Affirmation: My story is growing, just like me. I add new pages all the time.
Video Description: YouTube: 'The Dot' by Peter Reynolds read-aloud — about being willing to see yourself differently and discovering new capacities. Runtime ~8 min. Companion book: 'Beautiful Oops' by Barney Saltzberg — about reinterpreting old 'mistakes' as the beginning of something new.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: An old photograph — slightly faded. A child younger, smaller, less sure. VOICE: 'That was true then.' CUT TO: Same child now — new photo. Taller, more confident, more themselves. VOICE: 'But look who's here now.' CUT TO: Child adding to their photo album. New pages, new pictures, new story. VOICE: 'Your story is still being written. And you're the one holding the pen.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The photo album exercise is deeply affirming — let children spend real time on Page 4 (the new, updated picture of themselves). Display them in the room if children are happy to. Celebrate growth explicitly and specifically. This is one of the most joyful sessions of Phase 2.

Core Concept: We've been on the second part of our big adventure — learning how to put down some heavy things, say sorry properly, be brave about our fears, and start telling new stories about ourselves. Today we celebrate everything we've let go — and get excited for the next part of the journey: building!
Opening Hook: What is one heavy thing you've put down or made lighter during Phase 2? Maybe something you stopped worrying about as much. Something you said sorry for and felt better. A fear you were brave about. A story you started telling differently.
Signal Metaphor: Remember how our backpack got lighter in Phase 2? Today we check what we've taken out of it — the heavy things we chose to put down. And we get ready to fill it with new, brilliant things in Phase 3.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old adventure stories, there's always a moment between battles — a camp, a rest, a celebration. The heroes look at each other and say 'we made it through.' Not because the adventure is over — but because this part is done. And they're stronger for it. Today is that moment.
Teaching Points: 1. You've done SO much brave work in Phase 2. You've thought about forgiveness, about being yourself, about your fears, about the stories you tell yourself. | 2. It takes real courage to look at the heavy things and start putting them down. | 3. Today we celebrate all of that work. And we look forward to Phase 3 — where we get to BUILD new things! | 4. You are braver, wiser, and more yourself than you were 13 weeks ago. That is something to be really proud of.
Experiential Exercise: PHASE 2 CELEBRATION: Each child gets a paper 'heavy stone' and a paper 'feather.' On the stone, they write one heavy thing they've worked on putting down. On the feather, they write one thing that feels lighter now. Create a class display: all the stones in a pile, all the feathers flying around it. Read out the feathers together (keeping stones private). Celebrate every single one. Then: give each child a fresh blank page for Phase 3. 'Now we build.'
Guided Reflection: Hold your stone and your feather. Close your eyes. Notice how the feather feels compared to the stone. Now think: you chose to put some of the stone down. You made that choice. That was all you. How does it feel to know you can do that?
Journaling Prompt: Draw a picture of yourself lighter — after putting down something heavy. What does your face look like? How do you stand?
Weekly Practice (Mon): Celebrate one thing you're proud of from Phase 2. Tell someone about it!
Weekly Practice (Wed): Show a grown-up your stone and feather. Tell them about the heavy thing you've been working on and the lighter thing you feel now.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Come to the first Phase 3 session ready to tell us the most exciting thing you're going to BUILD!
Core Affirmation: I put down some heavy things. And now my hands are free to build something new.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'growth and change kids celebration animated' for an uplifting short about completing a challenging journey. Runtime ~3–5 min. Book: 'The Journey' by Francesca Sanna — a beautiful book about carrying what matters and leaving behind what doesn't.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A child walking — but look, the backpack is noticeably lighter. VOICE: 'Something changed.' CUT TO: The stone on the ground — set down, not dragged. The feather rising. VOICE: 'They chose to put something down. That was brave.' CUT TO: Child looking forward. A new horizon. Something being built in the distance. VOICE: 'Phase 3 begins. And your hands are finally free.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE — Phase 3: Rebuild.
Facilitator Notes: Make this session genuinely celebratory — balloons, music, something special. Children have done profound work in Phase 2. The stone/feather display is beautiful — photograph it and share with families. The transition to Phase 3 should feel like a genuine adventure beginning. Pure excitement.

Weekly Theme: Who Are You Now? — Rebuilding Identity
Core Concept: We've been on a huge adventure learning about ourselves — now comes the most exciting part: BUILDING! Today we start thinking about who we are CHOOSING to be — the qualities and values that make us most us — and how to grow more of them.
Opening Hook: If you could choose the most important qualities about yourself — things like kindness, courage, creativity, honesty, curiosity — what would you choose? What matters most to you?
Signal Metaphor: You've been finding out all about yourself — what you feel, what you carry, what you can put down. Now it's like you have a blank building site. And you get to decide what to build! Today we start designing.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In building stories, the best heroes are always the ones who discover who they truly are — not because someone told them, but because they chose it. Chose their values, chose their courage, chose their kindness. Today we start choosing.
Teaching Points: 1. You get to choose the kind of person you are becoming. That is one of the most exciting powers anyone has. | 2. The choices you make every day — how you treat people, what you pay attention to, what you practise — all build who you are. | 3. You already have wonderful qualities. And you can always build more. | 4. Today we start thinking about the qualities we most want to grow — and how we'll practise them.
Experiential Exercise: THE QUALITY BUILDER: Each child gets a brick-wall template (8–10 bricks). In each brick, they write or draw a quality they want to build in themselves — courage, kindness, creativity, perseverance, honesty, curiosity, etc. Then: circle the three most important ones. These are the foundations of their personal rebuild. Share: their three foundation bricks. Facilitator writes a class collective wall — all the bricks together.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think about the most important quality you want to build. Imagine yourself — in one year — with a lot more of that quality. What does that version of you look like? How do they treat people? How do they handle hard things? How do they feel? That version of you is possible. You're building toward it now.
Journaling Prompt: Draw a picture of 'Future Me' — the version of you with all the qualities you're building. What does that person look like?
Weekly Practice (Mon): Today, practise one of your foundation qualities in one real situation. Notice how it feels.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about your three foundation bricks. Ask them what theirs would be.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back your brick wall and add new bricks you've discovered this week!
Core Affirmation: I am choosing who I am building. My qualities are mine to grow.
Video Description: YouTube: 'What Do You Do With an Idea?' read-aloud by Kobi Yamada — about nurturing what you are building from the inside out. Runtime ~8 min. Book: 'Beautiful Me' by Kimberly and James Dean — affirming exploration of who you choose to be.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A cartoon building site — cleared and ready. VOICE: 'Phase 1 — we looked at everything. Phase 2 — we put down some heavy things. Now?' CUT TO: A child in a hard hat, surveying the site with excitement. VOICE: 'Now we build.' CUT TO: First brick laid — a word written on it. 'KINDNESS.' Another. 'COURAGE.' Another. 'CURIOSITY.' VOICE: 'That is your foundation. You choose every brick.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The building metaphor is enormously energising at this age — make it as physical and visual as possible. The collective class wall of qualities displayed in the room is a powerful image of community values. Keep the energy high — this is the most fun phase of the year.

Core Concept: Values are like the most important rules you make for yourself — not rules from other people, but the things YOU decide are most important about how you live and treat others. Today we find out what YOUR most important values are.
Opening Hook: What is the most important rule YOU have made for yourself — something you believe about how to treat people or how to live? Not a rule from school or home — something that feels most like yours.
Signal Metaphor: Imagine you have a special compass inside you — and instead of pointing to north, it points to what matters most to you. Today we find out which direction your compass actually points.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, the bravest heroes always had a strong inner compass — they knew what mattered, and they stuck to it even when things got hard. That compass was their values. Today we discover ours.
Teaching Points: 1. Values are the things that matter most to us — what we believe is important about how we live and treat others. | 2. Everyone's values are a little different — and that's what makes the world rich and interesting. | 3. Some common values are: kindness, honesty, courage, fairness, creativity, friendship, family, fun, learning, helping others. | 4. Knowing your values helps you make good decisions — when something feels wrong, it usually means it goes against one of your values.
Experiential Exercise: THE VALUES COMPASS: Each child gets a large compass drawn on paper (pointing N, S, E, W). In the four directions, they write or draw their four most important values. Facilitator shares examples and helps with vocabulary. Then: present dilemmas and ask children to use their compass: 'Your friend asks you to keep a secret that worries you — which value guides you?' / 'Someone is being left out — which value helps you decide what to do?' Share: your compass and your most important direction.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think about the value that feels MOST important to you. When have you lived it really well? How did it feel? Now think: when did you NOT live it and felt bad afterwards? What happened? Your compass was trying to guide you. Today we make it stronger.
Journaling Prompt: Draw your inner compass. Write your four most important values in the four directions. Decorate it so it looks like YOU.
Weekly Practice (Mon): When you face a choice today, use your compass: 'Which of my values guides me here?' Tell someone about it.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Show your compass to a grown-up. Tell them about the values you chose. Ask them what their compass points to.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring your compass back! Did you use it this week? What happened?
Core Affirmation: My values are my compass. They help me know who I am and how to treat others.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'values for kids animated' or 'what are values children' for short accessible content. Runtime ~5 min. Book: 'Those Shoes' by Maribeth Boelts — a beautiful story about knowing what you truly value versus what you want because others have it.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A cartoon compass, spinning. Gradually it slows and settles — pointing to a glowing word: KINDNESS. VOICE: 'That's what matters most to them. That's their compass.' CUT TO: Child at a moment of decision. Looks at their internal compass. It points clearly. VOICE: 'When you know what matters to you, decisions get clearer.' CUT TO: Child making the values-aligned choice. Looking peaceful. VOICE: 'Your compass is already inside you. Today you just learned to read it.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The compass is a brilliant physical metaphor — make it beautiful and keep it as a year-round tool. Present the dilemmas with warmth and humour. The discovery that values-based decisions feel better than approval-seeking decisions is a genuine revelation for this age.

Core Concept: Habits are things we practise so often they become automatic — we do them without even thinking. Today we think about the habits that GROW us — the small things we do every day that make us more of who we want to be.
Opening Hook: What is something you already do every day that has made you better at something or made you feel good about yourself? (Reading, practising a sport, being kind, helping someone.) How did that habit start?
Signal Metaphor: Think about how a plant grows. It doesn't shoot up all at once — it grows a tiny bit every single day. Good habits are like watering a plant. A little bit, every day, makes something beautiful grow.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories about people who became truly great — kind, wise, brave, skilled — it was never from one magic moment. It was always from small, consistent practice. Every single day. A little bit. That's how greatness actually grows.
Teaching Points: 1. A habit is something you do so regularly that it becomes almost automatic. | 2. The habits we practise build who we are — a little bit at a time. | 3. Even tiny habits matter! Five minutes of reading every day adds up to over 30 hours in a year. | 4. The best habits are ones that help us grow into the person we want to be.
Experiential Exercise: THE HABIT GARDEN: Each child gets a garden template with 3 plant pots. In each pot, they draw or write a small daily habit they want to grow — something that will help them build one of their quality-bricks from Week 27. Then they write: what's the SMALLEST daily version? (E.g. 'I will read for 5 minutes before bed' / 'I will say one kind thing to someone every day' / 'I will draw something for 3 minutes.'). Share: their three habit seeds and the smallest daily version of each.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Imagine watering your three habit plants every single day for three months. Picture them growing — slowly, steadily. What does your garden look like after three months? How do YOU feel? That garden is available to you. Starting today.
Journaling Prompt: Draw your habit garden in full — name the plants, draw how they might look when they've grown!
Weekly Practice (Mon): Start ONE of your habit plants today — the tiniest version. Just begin. Tell someone about it tonight.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Show a grown-up your habit garden. Ask them what habit they wish they had started when they were your age.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back: how many days did you water your habit plant? What happened?
Core Affirmation: Small daily habits grow into big wonderful things. I water my garden every day.
Video Description: YouTube: 'The Power of Yet' animated — Carol Dweck for kids, about the habit of persisting. Runtime ~5 min. Book: 'Little Acorn Becomes a Tree' or 'What a Seed Knows' for the growth metaphor. Also: 'Dreamers' by Yuyi Morales — about slow, persistent building.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: Three empty pots on a windowsill. VOICE: 'Nothing in them yet.' CUT TO: Day 1 — a child adds a tiny seed. Day 7 — tiny shoots. Day 30 — real plants. Day 90 — flourishing. VOICE: 'They didn't do anything dramatic. Just a little bit, every day.' CUT TO: The child smiling at their garden. VOICE: 'That's a habit. And habits grow exactly like plants — slowly, steadily, beautifully.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The garden metaphor is perfect for this age — consider having small actual seed packets as a physical take-home that mirrors the metaphor. The minimum habit concept ('just the tiniest version') dramatically reduces the activation energy. Send a habit tracking sheet home for family engagement.

Core Concept: Our bodies are the most amazing machines — they need certain things to work really well: good sleep, movement, healthy food, and ways to calm down when we feel stressed. Today we learn how to take care of our bodies so they can help us feel and be our best.
Opening Hook: Can you tell when your body needs more sleep? How do you feel? What about when you haven't moved around enough — how does that feel? What about when you've eaten mostly sugary things all day? Your body sends signals — let's learn to read them.
Signal Metaphor: Think of your body like a superhero suit. When it's charged up — with sleep, movement, good food, and calm — it can do extraordinary things. When it's running on empty, even superpowers don't work properly! Today we learn how to charge up.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: Ancient peoples knew something important: a well-rested, well-moved, well-nourished body thinks more clearly, feels more balanced, and has more courage. They were right — and now science confirms it. Today we learn the four things that charge our superhero suit.
Teaching Points: 1. Your body needs four things to work really well: SLEEP (to grow, learn, and feel okay), MOVEMENT (to feel energised and happy), GOOD FOOD (to have energy and think clearly), and CALM (ways to settle down when things feel overwhelming). | 2. When we don't get enough of these, everything gets harder — it's harder to concentrate, control our feelings, and be kind to others. | 3. The good news: even small improvements in any of these four things can make a big difference. | 4. Taking care of your body is one of the kindest things you can do for yourself AND for everyone around you.
Experiential Exercise: SUPERHERO SUIT CHECK: Each child rates their four areas with a simple traffic light (red/orange/green): Sleep, Movement, Food, Calm-Down Skills. Then for their most orange or red area: 'What is ONE small thing I could do to give this area a bit more green?' Facilitator works through examples: sleep (same bedtime every night, dark room), movement (playing outside, dancing, walking), food (one more piece of fruit, water before lunch), calm (three deep breaths, a favourite calming activity). Share: one upgrade they're committing to.
Guided Reflection: Let's practise charging our suits right now. Everyone: sit up tall, put both feet on the floor, take three slow deep breaths. Breathe in while I count to 4 — and out while I count to 6. Did you feel something shift? That's your calm-down power — and it works any time, any place.
Journaling Prompt: Draw your superhero suit charged up and ready. Label the four charging stations around it.
Weekly Practice (Mon): Try ONE of your charging habits today — and notice how it affects how you feel.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about the four charging areas. Ask them which one they find hardest to keep charged. Compare answers!
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back your superhero suit drawing — has anything changed in your charging levels?
Core Affirmation: When I take care of my body, I can be the best version of me. Sleep, movement, food, and calm — my four superchargers.
Video Description: YouTube: 'Sesame Street Belly Breathe' or search 'kids movement and sleep importance animated' for fun accessible content on body care for children. Runtime ~3–5 min. Book: 'I Am Yoga' by Susan Verde — a beautiful mindful body awareness book.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A cartoon superhero suit — four charging stations around it labelled SLEEP, MOVEMENT, FOOD, CALM. All four gauges low. Suit hanging limply. VOICE: 'When the suit isn't charged... it's really hard to do anything super.' CUT TO: Same suit, gradually charging as each station lights up. VOICE: 'Sleep — charging. Movement — charging. Good food — charging. Calm — charging.' CUT TO: Fully charged suit, glowing. Child puts it on. Stands tall. VOICE: 'That's how you charge your superpower.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The superhero charging metaphor is endlessly engaging for this age. Make the breathing practice a regular feature of every session from this point forward — 3 breaths to open each session. Involve families in the four charging areas — send a visual home they can put on the fridge.

Core Concept: The people we spend time with help shape who we become — because we learn from them, we pick up their habits and feelings, and we become more ourselves (or less ourselves) depending on who we're around. Today we think about the people in our lives who help us grow — and how to be that kind of person for others.
Opening Hook: Think of a friend or person who makes you feel really good — more yourself, happier, braver. What is it about them that makes you feel that way? What do they do that helps you grow?
Signal Metaphor: Think about how flowers grow better when they're planted near other healthy plants — they share good soil, they shelter each other from wind, and they make each other more beautiful. People work the same way! The right friends help us grow. Today we think about what makes a growing friendship.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories the best companions were always the ones who brought out the best in the hero — who believed in them, told them the truth, and stood by them through hard times. That kind of friendship is worth finding AND worth being. Today we think about both.
Teaching Points: 1. The people we spend the most time with have a big influence on how we feel and who we become. | 2. Growing friends are people who make us feel good about ourselves, encourage us to try new things, and are kind even when things are hard. | 3. We can also BE growing friends for others — by being kind, honest, encouraging, and supportive. | 4. It's okay if not everyone is a growing friend — but it's really worth finding and keeping the ones who are.
Experiential Exercise: THE GROWING FRIEND GARDEN: Each child gets a garden template with space for 3–4 friends. For each friend: draw or write their name, one thing they do that helps you grow, and one thing you do that helps THEM grow. Then: draw yourself in the garden too. What do you bring to your friendships? Share: one growing friend and one thing they bring to you.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think about your most growing friend — the one who makes you feel most like yourself. How do they make you feel? What do they do that helps? Now: what do YOU do for them? Are you being a growing friend back? What's one more thing you could do for them?
Journaling Prompt: Draw a picture showing you and a growing friend doing something together. What makes this friendship a growing one?
Weekly Practice (Mon): Do something kind or encouraging for a growing friend today — and notice how it feels to give as well as receive.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about one of your growing friends and why they matter to you. Ask them about their growing friends.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back a story about something a growing friend did for you this week — or something you did for them!
Core Affirmation: I choose friends who help me grow — and I am a growing friend for others.
Video Description: YouTube: 'Charlotte's Web' book read-aloud clips or search 'friendship for kids animated' for short content on what makes a good friend. Runtime ~5–8 min. Book: 'The Invisible String' by Patrice Karst — about the connections that matter most.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A garden — some plants growing vigorously side by side, supporting each other. Others struggling in poor soil, alone. VOICE: 'Plants grow better with the right companions. So do people.' CUT TO: Two children doing something together — laughing, exploring, genuinely enjoying each other. VOICE: 'A growing friend is someone who makes you more of who you are. Not less.' CUT TO: One child doing something kind for the other. VOICE: 'And the best thing about growing friends? You can be one too.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The growing friend concept should be kept warm and affirmative — this is not about judging friendships but about celebrating the ones that genuinely nourish. Acknowledge that all friendships have ups and downs. The seed activity (doing one kind thing for a growing friend) should have a real follow-through plan.

Core Concept: We've been building our inner coach — the kind, honest voice inside us. This week we practise using that voice every day. Today we design our personal 'power phrases' — the things we say to ourselves that help us feel brave, kind, and capable.
Opening Hook: What is the most helpful thing a kind voice could say to you when you're having a hard day? When you've made a mistake? When you're about to try something scary? What do you most need to hear?
Signal Metaphor: Remember your inner coach from a few weeks ago? Today we give them some really good lines. The best coaches always have just the right thing to say. Today we write ours.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, the bravest characters would say something to themselves before a challenge — a promise to themselves, a reminder of who they were. Those words became their power. Today we find ours.
Teaching Points: 1. The words we say to ourselves matter — they're heard more than any other voice we'll ever hear. | 2. When we practise saying kind, honest, encouraging things to ourselves, it actually changes how we feel and how brave we can be. | 3. Power phrases aren't magic — they're reminders of what's true about us when we forget. | 4. Today we create our own personal power phrases — the ones that are most true for us.
Experiential Exercise: POWER PHRASE CREATOR: Guide children through three types of power phrase: 1. BRAVE phrase (for when something feels scary): e.g. 'I can be scared AND brave at the same time.' 2. KIND phrase (for when you've made a mistake): e.g. 'I made a mistake. That doesn't make me bad. I can try again.' 3. STRONG phrase (for hard days): e.g. 'I am doing my best, and that is enough.' Each child writes their own version of each type — in their own words. Share: their brave phrase with the group.
Guided Reflection: Let's practise our brave phrases right now. Everyone close their eyes. Think of something that feels a bit scary. Now say your brave phrase to yourself — quietly, in your head. How does it feel? Take a breath. Say it again. Notice what changes.
Journaling Prompt: Write or decorate your three power phrases on a card to keep. Make it beautiful — it's important!
Weekly Practice (Mon): Use your brave phrase today — even if nothing scary happens, just practise saying it.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Teach a grown-up your three power phrases. Ask them what THEIR power phrases are.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back your power phrase card! Which one did you use most this week?
Core Affirmation: I have words that help me. I say them to myself with kindness and truth.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'positive self-talk for kids animated' or 'affirmations for children YouTube' for short, accessible animations. Runtime ~5 min. Book: 'I Am Enough' by Grace Byers — a beautiful collection of affirmations in picture book form.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A child before something scary — about to give a speech, try something new. We hear the worried inner voice. VOICE: 'That's the old voice. Let's try a different one.' CUT TO: Child closes eyes. Says their brave phrase quietly. Breathes. Opens eyes. VOICE: 'Not the magic disappearing of fear. The brave choosing to go anyway.' CUT TO: Child doing the thing — imperfectly, real, proud. VOICE: 'Power phrases don't remove the challenge. They remind you who you are while you face it.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: Create beautiful, laminated power phrase cards for children to take home — make them special objects, not just worksheets. Involve parents: send a note explaining power phrases and asking them to use the same language at home. The three-category structure (brave, kind, strong) covers the most important emotional situations.

Core Concept: Having a routine — a regular order for how we do things — actually helps us feel safer, calmer, and more able to enjoy the fun parts of our day. Today we think about the routines that help us the most — and maybe design some new ones.
Opening Hook: What's a routine you have that really helps you? Maybe a bedtime routine, or how you get ready in the morning, or something you do after school? Why does it help?
Signal Metaphor: Think about how a garden grows best when it has a good watering routine, the right amount of sunshine each day, and regular weeding. Your life grows best when it has a good routine too! Today we design our personal growth garden routine.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, the wisest people always had a rhythm to their days — they knew when to work, when to rest, when to play, and when to think. That rhythm didn't make their days boring. It made everything else possible.
Teaching Points: 1. Having a routine — a regular order for important parts of the day — helps our brains feel safe and our bodies feel settled. | 2. When we know what's coming, we have more energy for the fun, creative, and unexpected parts of life. | 3. A good daily routine includes time for sleep, movement, food, learning, connection, and rest. | 4. Today we think about what our ideal daily rhythm looks like — and pick one small routine to strengthen.
Experiential Exercise: MY DAILY RHYTHM: Give each child a simple clock/timeline template for a day. Together, fill in the key anchors: wake time, breakfast, school or activity, movement time, connection time (family/friends), quiet or creative time, bedtime. Then: 'Is there one part of your day that feels chaotic or hard? Could a small routine help?' Design one new mini-routine for that part. Share: their new mini-routine.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Imagine your perfect calm day — everything in a good rhythm. What time do you wake up? What makes mornings feel good? What do you do after school? What helps you sleep? Notice how calm it feels when your day has a good rhythm. You can build that.
Journaling Prompt: Draw your ideal daily rhythm as a clock or timeline. What are the most important parts?
Weekly Practice (Mon): Try your new mini-routine today. Notice how it feels to have that part of your day feel more settled.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about your new mini-routine. Ask them to help you stick to it this week.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back: how did your mini-routine go? Did it help?
Core Affirmation: A good daily rhythm helps me feel calm, settled, and ready for anything.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'daily routine for kids animated' for short, engaging content about healthy daily rhythms. Runtime ~5 min. Book: 'Bedtime for Frances' by Russell Hoban — gently illustrates the importance of routine and what happens when it's disrupted.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A cartoon day without any rhythm — chaotic, scattered, ending in a tired, grumpy child. VOICE: 'No rhythm. Everything's harder.' CUT TO: Same child, next day — with a simple morning routine and a bedtime rhythm. Calmer. More settled. VOICE: 'Same child. A little more rhythm.' CUT TO: Child at bedtime, peaceful and ready. VOICE: 'Routines don't take away the adventure. They make it easier to have one.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: Coordinate with parents for this session — family buy-in on routine changes is essential for children. Focus on one small, achievable routine improvement rather than a whole-day redesign. Sleep routine is the highest-leverage area for most primary-age children. Send home a simple routine template families can use together.

Weekly Theme: Rest as a Practice, Not a Reward
Core Concept: Rest is not just sleep — it's also the quiet, gentle times when our brain and body get to recover and refuel. Today we learn about the importance of rest, what real rest looks and feels like, and how to give our brain the recovery time it needs.
Opening Hook: What do you do when you want to relax and feel better? What makes you feel most refreshed and restored? Is it different to what you do when you're bored?
Signal Metaphor: Think about a phone that's been on all day with lots of apps open. By the evening, it's hot and the battery is nearly empty. People are the same! Our brains need quiet time — not just sleep, but gentle, calm recovery time during the day.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, even the greatest heroes had to rest before the big challenge. Not because they were weak — but because they were wise enough to know that the body and mind need recovery time to do their best. Rest is a superpower, not a sign of being lazy.
Teaching Points: 1. Rest is not the same as sleep — it's also the quiet time your brain needs during the day to process everything it's learned and feel settled. | 2. Some things we think are rest — like watching lots of videos or scrolling — actually keep our brains busy. Real rest is quieter. | 3. Real rest might look like: playing outside, drawing, listening to music, daydreaming, quiet reading, or just being still for a few minutes. | 4. When we rest properly, we can think more clearly, feel calmer, and actually enjoy things more.
Experiential Exercise: REST vs. BUSY BREAK: Show children two lists and sort together: REST (quiet reading, outdoor play, drawing, daydreaming, calm music, gentle movement) vs. BUSY BREAK (lots of screens, fast-paced games, scrolling, loud noise). Discuss: how does each feel in your body? How do you feel after each? Then: design your personal 'rest menu' — three go-to genuine rest activities that work for YOU. Share: their top rest activity.
Guided Reflection: Let's practise right now. Everyone: sit or lie comfortably. Close your eyes if you want. For 2 minutes, just breathe and let your mind wander wherever it wants — no thinking about anything on purpose. Just... rest. When we open our eyes: how did that feel?
Journaling Prompt: Draw your 'rest menu' — three activities that give your brain real rest. Make it beautiful!
Weekly Practice (Mon): Take a genuine rest break today — from your rest menu. Notice how you feel before and after.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Show a grown-up your rest menu. Ask them what rest looks like for them. Plan a rest time together this week.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back: which rest activity did you try? How did it feel?
Core Affirmation: Real rest is when my brain gets to breathe. It makes everything else better.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'rest for kids why it matters animated' or 'why do we need rest children YouTube' for short accessible content. Runtime ~5 min. Book: 'The Rabbit Listened' by Cori Doerrfeld — about the kind of quiet presence that genuinely restores.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A brain in cartoon form — hot, busy, lots of things spinning. VOICE: 'This brain has been working really hard. It needs something.' CUT TO: The child sitting outside, looking at clouds. Brain slowly cooling, spinning things slowing. VOICE: 'That. Right there. That's rest.' CUT TO: Brain, refreshed. Everything a bit clearer, a bit calmer, a bit more ready. VOICE: 'Rest isn't doing nothing. It's giving your brain what it needs.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The rest menu is a lovely, practical take-home from this session. The 2-minute rest practice in the session is worth doing slowly and genuinely — model it yourself. Coordinate with parents to support genuine rest practices at home, distinct from screen time. The rest/busy-break distinction is a powerful concept for both children and parents.

Core Concept: Making things — drawing, building, writing, singing, dancing, inventing — is one of the most wonderful things human beings can do. And everyone can do it! Today we celebrate creativity, remember what we love to make, and give ourselves permission to create without worrying about whether it's perfect.
Opening Hook: What is your absolute favourite thing to make or create? Drawing? Building? Writing? Dancing? Making music? Something else? What does it feel like when you're deep in making something you love?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine if every time you drew a picture, someone graded it. Or every time you made up a song, someone told you it wasn't good enough. You'd probably stop trying! Today we remember that making things is for the joy of making — not for getting it right.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: The most creative people in history — inventors, artists, storytellers — all had one thing in common: they were willing to make things that weren't perfect. In fact, most of their greatest creations came out of lots of imperfect attempts. Today we celebrate the imperfect making.
Teaching Points: 1. Making things is one of the most important things humans do — it's how we express who we are and what matters to us. | 2. There is no right or wrong way to be creative — your way is always the right way. | 3. The best creative experiences happen when we make for the joy of it — not to impress anyone or get it perfect. | 4. Everyone is creative. Creativity looks different for different people — and all of it is valuable.
Experiential Exercise: THE MAKING PARTY: Facilitate a free-choice creative session — provide a range of materials (drawing supplies, building blocks, collage materials, writing paper, musical instruments if available). For 15 minutes, everyone makes something — anything they want, however they want. No instructions. No right answer. No evaluation. Then: share what you made — not for judgment but for celebration. Each share receives: 'Tell us about your making — what did you enjoy about it?' NOT 'That's so good!' (evaluation). Just genuine curiosity.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think about being deep in making something you love — completely absorbed, time flying, just you and the making. Remember that feeling. That feeling is available to you any time you pick up the thing that helps you make. It belongs to you. Nobody can take it.
Journaling Prompt: Make something today just for the joy of it — not to show anyone, not to get it right. Just because making things is wonderful.
Weekly Practice (Mon): Show a grown-up something you've made recently. Tell them about what you ENJOYED about making it — not whether you think it's good.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Bring something you've made this week to share — just to celebrate the making!
Weekly Practice (Sun): I am creative. Making things is part of how I am most alive. I make for joy.
Core Affirmation: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0ZcfX2862XE
Video Description: The Dot read-aloud by Peter H. Reynolds — a celebration of creative courage and the joy of making something just because. Runtime ~8 min. Companion book: 'Beautiful Oops' by Barney Saltzberg — a joyful celebration of imperfect making.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A blank table covered in paper and art supplies. Colours everywhere — markers, crayons, paint, glitter. VOICE (warm, excited): 'No rules. No right answer. Just making — for the joy of it.' CUT TO: A child's hands drawing a bright red swirl — then pausing, adding a line, smiling. VOICE: 'This is what it looks like when you let yourself create without worrying if it's good enough. It doesn't have to be perfect. It just has to be yours.' CUT TO: Many hands making different things — a wonky clay cup, a painting of a purple dog, a collage of magazine clippings. Each child absorbed in their own creation. FADE TO: The finished artwork — imperfect, personal, beautiful. VOICE: 'That feeling right there? That's the joy of making. Take it with you. Make more things.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE — The Joy of Making.
Facilitator Notes: The 15-minute making party is the centrepiece — protect that time. Let children experiment with different mediums. Display finished work on a 'gallery wall' and celebrate each piece individually. No critique — only noticing what you like about each creation.

Core Concept: Every person has gifts — things they're naturally good at, things they love, and ways they can help others. When we use our gifts to help and contribute, that's called purpose. Today we start discovering what our gifts are and how we can share them.
Opening Hook: What is something you love doing AND you're good at AND it helps other people? It might be something you haven't thought of as a gift before.
Signal Metaphor: Imagine the world is like a giant puzzle. Every single person is a piece. And the puzzle only works when every piece is in the right place, doing what it does best. Today we figure out what makes you the perfect YOU-shaped piece.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories about heroes and great people, they always had something special — a gift that was uniquely theirs. Not perfect. Not magical. Just genuinely theirs. And they used it to make things better. Today we find yours.
Teaching Points: 1. Everyone has gifts — things they love, things they're good at, and ways they can help others. | 2. Purpose means using your gifts to do something that matters — not just for yourself, but for others too. | 3. You don't need to have everything figured out. You just need to start noticing what feels most like you AND most helpful. | 4. Even small contributions matter enormously — being kind, helping a friend, making someone laugh, listening when someone is sad. These are purposes too.
Experiential Exercise: GIFT EXPLORER: Three prompts for each child to write or draw: 1. 'Something I love and I'm good at is...' 2. 'Something I do that seems to help or matter to others is...' 3. 'If I could change one thing about the world, I would...' Then: where do these overlap? That's the beginning of your purpose. Share: one gift they have that they want to use more.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think of a time when you did something that really helped someone — even something small. How did it feel? That feeling — of genuinely contributing something that mattered — that's the feeling of purpose. It's available to you every day, in small ways.
Journaling Prompt: Draw your 'YOU-shaped puzzle piece' — write your gifts inside it and draw how it connects to the people and world around you.
Weekly Practice (Mon): Use one of your gifts to help someone today. Notice how it feels.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about one of your gifts. Ask them what gift they think you have that you might not have noticed yet.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back your puzzle piece drawing — and a story about using one of your gifts this week!
Core Affirmation: I have gifts that are uniquely mine. Using them to help others is my purpose.
Video Description: YouTube: 'Wonder' read-aloud clips or search 'purpose for kids animated gifts' for short accessible content on contribution and gifts. Runtime ~5–8 min. Book: 'The Jelly That Wouldn't Wiggle' by Alexandra Parry — about each person's unique contribution to something bigger.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A giant puzzle — most pieces in place, but missing some. VOICE: 'Every puzzle needs every piece.' CUT TO: A child holding their puzzle piece — unique shape, something special written on it. VOICE: 'Your piece is the exact right shape for the space only you can fill.' CUT TO: The child places their piece. The picture becomes more complete. VOICE: 'That is purpose. Not a grand plan. Just your piece, in your place, doing what only you can do.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: Keep purpose concrete and immediately actionable for this age — not about the future, but about what they can contribute today. Celebrate every 'gift' that is shared generously and specifically. The puzzle metaphor reinforces both uniqueness AND interdependence — both are important values to embed.

Weekly Theme: Money, Abundance and Your Relationship With Resources
Session Title: What We Have and What We Share
Core Concept: Money is something that grown-ups think about a lot — and most children hear messages about it without fully understanding them. Today we think about what we've been taught about money and resources, and what a healthy, kind relationship with what we have looks like.
Opening Hook: What is something you have — that doesn't cost any money — that you're really grateful for? And what is something you own that you love sharing with others?
Signal Metaphor: Think about everything you have — your toys, your home, your food, your family, your friends. Some things cost money. Some things are free. Today we think about what really matters, how to be grateful for what we have, and how to be generous with what we can share.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, the happiest and wisest characters were never the ones who had the most things. They were the ones who valued what they had, shared generously, and knew the difference between what they needed and what they just wanted. Today we learn that wisdom.
Teaching Points: 1. Money is a tool — it helps us get things we need and some things we want. But it's not the most important thing in life. | 2. Gratitude — being thankful for what we have — makes us feel richer, even if we don't have very much. | 3. Generosity — sharing what we have — actually makes us feel happier and more connected. | 4. Learning the difference between things we NEED and things we WANT is one of the most important money skills there is.
Experiential Exercise: NEED vs. WANT vs. SHARE: Facilitate a sorting activity with picture cards or drawn items: sort into NEED (food, shelter, warmth, healthcare), WANT (toys, treats, gadgets), and COULD SHARE (time, kindness, skills, some possessions). Discuss: 'Is it possible to share something that doesn't cost money? What can you share that isn't a thing?' Then: each child identifies one thing they're grateful for, and one non-money thing they can share this week. Share: their chosen gratitude and their generous act.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think about everything you have — your home, your family, your friends, your health, your skills, your imagination. Even if it's hard sometimes, there is a lot there. Take a moment just to notice it and feel grateful. Now: is there something in that list you could share? Something that would cost you nothing but would mean a lot to someone else?
Journaling Prompt: Draw or write about three things you have that money can't buy — and three things you can share with others.
Weekly Practice (Mon): Do one generous act this week — something you give that doesn't cost money.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Ask a grown-up: 'What's something you have that you're really grateful for that money can't buy?' Share your answer with them too.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back: what generous act did you do this week? How did it feel?
Core Affirmation: I am grateful for what I have. And I am generous with what I can share.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'generosity for kids animated' or 'gratitude and giving children YouTube' for short accessible content. Runtime ~5 min. Book: 'Those Shoes' by Maribeth Boelts — a beautiful story about needs vs. wants and the joy of generosity.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A child's bedroom full of toys — but looking somehow empty. VOICE: 'All this — and something still feels like it's missing.' CUT TO: Same child sharing something with a friend. Simple. Not expensive. VOICE: 'There it is.' CUT TO: Both children laughing. Connected. VOICE: 'Gratitude and generosity — they're not about what you have. They're about how you relate to what you have.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: Be sensitive to varying financial circumstances among children — never compare or highlight differences. Focus on non-material forms of abundance (time, kindness, skills, imagination) which are genuinely available to all. The need/want/share activity is one of the most practically valuable financial literacy exercises for this age.

Core Concept: We all belong to communities — our family, our class, our sports team, our neighbourhood. A good community is one where people care for each other, help each other, and make each other feel like they belong. Today we think about the communities we're part of — and how to make them better.
Opening Hook: What communities are you part of? Name as many as you can — family, class, sports team, neighbourhood, this group. What makes each one special?
Signal Metaphor: Imagine a beehive. Every bee has a job. Every bee matters. When all the bees work together, they make something amazing that none of them could make alone. You are part of communities like beehives — and what you contribute matters.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, the strongest characters were always the ones who had good communities around them — people who cared, who helped, who showed up. And the strongest characters were also the ones who gave back — who contributed something that made their community better. Today we think about both.
Teaching Points: 1. A community is a group of people who care about each other and contribute to something together. | 2. Being part of a good community helps us feel safe, loved, and like we belong. | 3. Communities become stronger when everyone contributes — even small contributions matter enormously. | 4. You can make your communities better by being kind, showing up, including others, and contributing what you're good at.
Experiential Exercise: COMMUNITY BUILDER: Each child identifies two or three communities they belong to. For each: 'What does this community give me?' and 'What do I give to this community?' Then: 'Is there someone in one of my communities who might feel left out or could use more belonging? What is one thing I could do to include them or make them feel more part of things?' Share: one community they love and one thing they contribute to it.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think about your favourite community — the one where you feel most like you belong. What makes it feel like home? What do YOU bring to it that makes it better? Now: is there one person in that community who might need a bit more belonging? What could you do?
Journaling Prompt: Draw your favourite community. Write or draw what everyone in it contributes — including yourself.
Weekly Practice (Mon): Do one thing today that makes one of your communities a tiny bit better — include someone, help someone, contribute something.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about one of your communities and what you love about belonging to it. Ask them about their favourite community.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back: what did you do to make your community better this week? What happened?
Core Affirmation: I belong to communities that matter. And I make them better by contributing who I am.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'community and belonging for kids animated' or 'teamwork children YouTube' for accessible short content. Runtime ~5 min. Book: 'Last Stop on Market Street' by Matt de la Pena — a beautiful story about noticing and contributing to the community around you.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A cartoon beehive — every bee busy, contributing, the hive alive with purpose. VOICE: 'Every bee matters. Every contribution counts.' CUT TO: Child looking at their communities — family, class, this group. VOICE: 'You are part of beehives like this. And what you bring matters more than you know.' CUT TO: Child doing one small generous act in their community. Something shifting. More belonging. VOICE: 'Community isn't something you find. It's something you build — one kind act, one genuine contribution at a time.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The beehive metaphor is wonderful for group dynamics — every child can see themselves as essential. The 'someone who might need more belonging' prompt is powerful and should be handled with sensitivity — make it about outward reaching, not inward inventory of who is and isn't included.

Core Concept: We've been building for 13 weeks! Today we celebrate everything we've grown and built — and get ready for the most exciting phase yet: going out into the world and USING everything we've built to make things better.
Opening Hook: Let's go on a memory adventure through Phase 3! What are all the things we've built and grown in the last 13 weeks? (Identity, values compass, habit garden, superhero suit, growing friends, inner coach voice, daily rhythm, rest, creativity, purpose puzzle piece, community...)
Signal Metaphor: Remember the blank building site from Week 27? Today we look at what we've built on it — all the bricks and qualities and habits and friendships. And then we get ready for Phase 4: taking everything we've built out into the world and using it!
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In adventure stories, there always comes the moment when the hero has done the training, learned the skills, found their team — and it's time to go. Not because they're perfect. Because they're ready enough, and the world needs what they have. Today is that moment.
Teaching Points: 1. You've built SO much in Phase 3 — a stronger identity, clearer values, new habits, a better relationship with your body and rest, creative expression, a sense of purpose, and deeper community. | 2. These things are yours. You built them. Nobody can take them away. | 3. Phase 4 is the most exciting phase: it's about using everything you've built to contribute to the world around you — your family, your community, and beyond. | 4. You are more ready than you know. And the world genuinely needs what you have to give.
Experiential Exercise: PHASE 3 CELEBRATION TOWER: Each child gets a series of 'brick' cards (one per Phase 3 theme). They write one thing they built in each brick. Stack the bricks into a tower. Display all the towers together — the visual of everything built. Then: add one 'door' brick at the top of each tower: 'Phase 4 — what I'm bringing into the world.' Share: their most important brick and what's written on their door.
Guided Reflection: Hold your tower. Close your eyes. Feel how much heavier it is than the empty site at the start. Look at everything you've added. These are real. These are yours. You built these through showing up, week after week, honestly and bravely. Now: you get to take everything in this tower and use it to make things better. That's Phase 4. Are you ready?
Journaling Prompt: Draw your building tower from Phase 3 — full, colourful, yours. What's written on the door at the top?
Weekly Practice (Mon): Celebrate one thing you built in Phase 3 today — use one of your Phase 3 tools in the real world.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Show a grown-up your tower. Tell them everything that's in it. Let them be genuinely amazed.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Come to the first Phase 4 session ready to tell us: what are you going to DO with everything you've built?
Core Affirmation: I built something real and strong. Now I get to take it into the world. Phase 4 — here I come!
Video Description: YouTube: 'Oh, the Places You'll Go!' read-aloud by Dr Seuss — the perfect send-off from building to living. Runtime ~8 min. Also: search 'children growth celebration animated YouTube' for uplifting content.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: The building site from Week 27 — now with a real building on it. Not perfect. Genuinely built. VOICE: 'Thirteen weeks ago — empty site. Today?' CUT TO: Children's brick towers, all different, all full, all brilliant. VOICE: 'Look at all of that. Built by you.' CUT TO: The door at the top of each tower opening — Phase 4 beyond. VOICE: 'Phase 4 isn't about developing more. It's about taking everything you built and giving it to the world.' CUT TO: Children walking through their doors together. VOICE: 'You are more ready than you know.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE — Phase 4: Live It.
Facilitator Notes: Make this session genuinely spectacular — this is the three-phase arc completing and Phase 4 beginning. Balloons, music, a visual display of all three phases' work together. Children should leave feeling genuinely proud, genuinely capable, and genuinely excited. The tower display is a beautiful artefact — photograph it and share with families.

Core Concept: We've spent all year learning about ourselves — our feelings, our habits, our strengths, and our values. Now comes the most exciting part: using everything we've learned to make things better for the people around us! Today we think about how to share our superpowers with the world.
Opening Hook: What is the most important thing you've learned about yourself this year? And who is one person in your life who could use that learning — who is going through something you've already learned about?
Signal Metaphor: Remember the backpack full of tools from Phase 1? And the building site from Phase 3? Today we take our tools and our building skills OUT into the world. We've been building ourselves up — now we build things UP for others too!
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, the hero's journey always ended the same way — not with the hero keeping all the treasure for themselves, but with them returning home and sharing it. The return and the sharing is the most important part. Today we begin our return.
Teaching Points: 1. One of the most amazing things about growing is that it doesn't just make YOU better — it makes you better for others too. | 2. When we've learned something important, sharing it with others is one of the most generous things we can do. | 3. Service doesn't have to be big or grand. It can be as simple as being kind when someone needs it, sharing what you've learned, or showing up for someone who's struggling. | 4. When we give from our strengths — from what we've genuinely built — it feels amazing. That's called giving from fullness.
Experiential Exercise: TREASURE MAP: Each child gets a treasure map template. They mark three 'treasures' they've gathered this year — the most important things they've learned or built. Then they draw a path from the treasure to someone who could benefit from it. For each treasure: who would benefit? What specifically would you give them — a kindness, a conversation, a skill, an example? Share: their most important treasure and who they want to give it to.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think of someone you know who is finding something difficult — something you've learned about this year. Imagine yourself going to them and sharing what you know. Not bossy — just kind. Sharing your treasure. How does it feel to imagine giving something that helps? That feeling? That's what service feels like.
Journaling Prompt: Draw yourself giving one of your treasures to someone who needs it. What are you giving? What happens when they receive it?
Weekly Practice (Mon): Do one act of genuine service today — give one of your treasures to someone who needs it.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Tell a grown-up about one treasure you want to share and who you want to give it to. Ask them to help you do it.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back: what treasure did you share this week? What happened?
Core Affirmation: I have treasures to share. Giving them to others is one of the best things I can do.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'kindness for kids animated service' or read-aloud of 'Each Kindness' by Jacqueline Woodson — about the treasure of kindness and what it does when you share it. Runtime ~8 min.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A child's backpack — full of treasures gathered across the year. VOICE: 'Look at everything in there. Built over a whole year.' CUT TO: Child opening the backpack and looking outward — toward others. VOICE: 'Now the best part.' CUT TO: Child sharing a treasure with a friend. Something glowing between them. VOICE: 'Giving what you have built — that is the most important part of the adventure.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: This session should feel genuinely joyful — the year's arc completing in outward giving. The treasure map activity is beautiful and can be displayed. Keep the service concrete and age-appropriate. Celebrate every act of giving that is shared back.

Core Concept: One of the best ways to really know something is to teach it to someone else. Today we practise sharing the things we've learned this year — with our families, our friends, and our community. When we teach, we learn even more deeply!
Opening Hook: What is one thing you've learned this year that you could teach to a younger child — or to a grown-up who had never heard of it? What would you say?
Signal Metaphor: Have you ever explained something to a younger child and realised you understood it much better after you explained it? That's because teaching is one of the best ways to really know something. Today we become teachers!
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: In old stories, wisdom was always passed on — from elder to young, from those who'd learned to those just beginning. Today we practise that. You have wisdom to pass on. More than you know.
Teaching Points: 1. Teaching something to someone else helps US understand it better too — not just them. | 2. You have learned so much this year — about feelings, habits, values, courage, kindness, community. All of that is worth sharing. | 3. Teaching doesn't have to be in a classroom. It can be a conversation, a drawing, a story, or just showing someone by how you act. | 4. The best teachers share from their own experience — not just facts, but what it actually felt like to learn something.
Experiential Exercise: MINI TEACHER: Each child prepares a 2-minute 'lesson' to share with the group. They choose one thing they've learned this year — any concept from any session — and explain it in their own words with an example. Facilitator gives 5 minutes to prepare. Then each child shares their lesson. Group responses: 'What I understood from that was...' and 'One question I have is...' Celebrate every share generously.
Guided Reflection: Close your eyes. Think about everything you've learned this year. Now: if a brand new friend joined this group today and hadn't been on the whole journey with you, what's the ONE most important thing you'd want them to know? How would you explain it? That is your teaching gift.
Journaling Prompt: Write or draw your 'lesson' from today in a simple way that someone younger could understand. Give it a title!
Weekly Practice (Mon): Teach one thing from this year to someone at home today — a parent, sibling, or anyone who'll listen. Notice how it feels.
Weekly Practice (Wed): Ask a grown-up: 'Can I teach you something I learned this year?' Then teach them. Watch their face.
Weekly Practice (Sun): Bring back: who did you teach? What happened? Did you learn anything new by teaching it?
Core Affirmation: I have things worth teaching. When I share what I know, I learn it even more deeply.
Video Description: YouTube: Search 'kids teaching each other learning animated' or 'peer learning children YouTube' for accessible short content. Runtime ~5 min. Book: 'The One and Only Ivan' — about passing on what you know to those who come after.
Film Script (2min Narration): FADE IN: A child standing up confidently, explaining something to a group. Not perfectly. Genuinely. VOICE: 'They've been the student all year. Now watch.' CUT TO: The group listening — genuinely interested, genuinely learning from their peer. VOICE: 'Teaching is not about being perfect. It is about passing on what is real.' CUT TO: The teacher-child, after. Something different in their face. More ownership. More depth. VOICE: 'They know it now in a way they didn't before. Because they gave it away.' FADE TO TITLE: Mindcast LIVE.
Facilitator Notes: The mini-teacher activity is one of the most joyful sessions of Phase 4 — children are genuinely proud of their knowledge. Give ample preparation time and make the sharing feel like a celebration, not a performance. Video the sessions with parental consent — children love watching themselves teach.

Session Title: The Real You, All the Way
Core Concept: Being seen means letting people know who you really are — not just the brave face or the happy face, but the real you, with all your feelings and ideas and wonderfulness. Today we practise the courage of being genuinely, fully ourselves in front of the people we care about.
Opening Hook: Think of a time when you showed up completely as yourself — no pretending, no performing — and something really good happened because of it. What was that like?
Signal Metaphor: Remember the mask craft from way back? We talked about real faces and pretend faces. Today, in Phase 4, we go all in on the real face. Not because it's always easy — but because the best friendships and the best moments happen when we show up as really, truly ourselves.
Ancient Wisdom Reframe: The bravest thing in old stories was never fighting a dragon. It was being honest — truly honest — about who you are, even when that felt scary. Because the truest connections happen when people see the real you and choose to be close to you anyway.
Teaching Points: 1. Being genuinely seen — letting people know who you really are — is one of the bravest things a person can do. | 2. The best friendships and relationships happen when people see the real us and love us anyway. | 3. It takes courage because we can't control how people respond. But the risk is worth it — because the friendships built on the real you are the strongest ones. | 4. You've spent all year building the real you. Phase 4 is about showing that real you to the world.
Experiential Exercise: THE REAL ME GALLERY: Each child creates a small 'gallery card' about themselves — their real self. Sections: My real name and one thing about it, One thing I love that people might not know, One thing I find hard that I'm working on, One thing I'm really proud of about myself, One way I want people to know me. Cards are displayed in a 'Real Me Gallery' around the room. Gallery walk — everyone reads each other's cards. Share: one thing from someone else's card that surprised or delighted you.
